Learning points: (1) “prompt” → “prompting” keeps the “p”; (2) consonant clusters (mpt) are common in English (tempt, exempt, prompt); (3) proofreading tip: check missing letters around consonant clusters; (4) “diversified” means made varied; (5) hyphen/em-dash punctuation doesn’t affect spelling validity.

questionsEn.q: Choose the misspelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: “Indelable” is misspelt; the correct word is “indelible” (meaning permanent; cannot be erased). The other options are correctly spelt. Learning points: (1) “indelible” often collocates with “impression/mark”; (2) suffix “-ible” (capable of) is common (visible, edible); (3) don’t confuse “delete” with “delible”—English uses “delible/indelible”; (4) spelling check: -elible not -elable; (5) “noticeable/portable/memorable” follow predictable -able endings.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “Satellite” (one “t”, one “l”, ends with “-ite”). The other options contain extra/missing letters. Learning points: common spelling traps include doubled consonants; break word into parts (satell-ite); verify vowel placement; read slowly for repeated letters.

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option 'No replacement required'.** The kitchen was **redolant** of spices, evoking memories of his grandmother's cooking.
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “redolent” meaning “strongly reminiscent or suggestive of” (often used with “of”). The sentence needs “redolent of spices”. “Redolant” is misspelt, and (b)/(c) are incorrect spellings. Learning points: collocation is “redolent of”; meaning link = “fragrant/suggestive”; replace only the misspelt target; “No replacement required” applies only if the underlined word is correct.

questionsEn.q: There are four underlined words in the sentence given below. One of them is misspelt. Choose the option with the misspelt word.** The court directed the authorities to ensure **equitable** distribution of **resources** and prevent any form of **discremination** against the **marginalised**.
questionsEn.s: The misspelt word in the sentence is **discremination**; the correct spelling is “discrimination”, which corresponds to option (c). The other underlined words are correctly spelt. Learning points: “discrimination” contains “-crim-” not “-crem-”; check underlined targets carefully; British spelling “marginalised” with “-ise” is acceptable; “equitable” relates to fairness, not equality.

questionsEn.q: Choose the misspelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: “Ambeince” is misspelt; the correct spelling is “Ambience” (meaning atmosphere). The other words are correctly spelt. Learning points: “-ience” ending in ambience; pronunciation can mislead spelling; compare with “science/patience”; double-check vowel order (ie/ei).

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is **mischievous** (meaning: playful in a slightly naughty way; causing minor trouble). (a) misses “ie,” (b) has incorrect ending, and (d) has incorrect vowel order. Learning points: (1) correct syllable pattern: mis-chie-vous, (2) adjective form; noun: “mischief,” (3) common confusion: people often pronounce an extra syllable (“mis-chee-vee-us”) but spelling remains “mischievous,” (4) use: “a mischievous grin.”

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option "No replacement required".** The **munificient** donation to the hospital ensured the construction of a state-of-the-art cancer wing.
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is **munificent** (meaning: very generous, especially in giving). The underlined word **munificient** is misspelt. (a) and (c) are incorrect spellings, and (d) is wrong because a correction is required. Learning points: (1) “munificent” relates to generosity; synonym: “bountiful,” (2) common collocations: “munificent donation/grant,” (3) spelling tip: ends with “-cent,” not “-cient,” (4) pronunciation: /mjuːˈnɪfɪs(ə)nt/.

test.instructions: Standard CBT Pattern Exam. Positive Marks: +1, Negative Marks: -0.25. Total Questions: 50.

test.title: Set - 8

questionsEn.q: There are four underlined words in the sentence given below. One of them is misspelt. Choose the option with the misspelt word.** **Journalists** raised concerns about government **censorship**, media freedom, and the rise of controlled **narratives** in national **broadcastes**.
questionsEn.s: The misspelt underlined word is the last one (shown as **broadcastes** in the sentence); the correct spelling is **broadcasts**. The other words—journalists, censorship, narratives—are correctly spelt. Learning points: (1) “broadcast” plural/3rd person singular often takes “-s”: broadcasts, (2) spelling check: no extra “e” before “s” here, (3) “narrative” means a story/interpretation, often used in media context, (4) proofreading strategy: verify suffixes (-s/-es) based on word endings.

questionsEn.q: Choose the misspelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: The misspelt word is **Profesional**; the correct spelling is **Professional** (double “s”). The other options are correctly spelt. Learning points: (1) “profession” → “professional” keeps the double “s,” (2) adjective form: professional conduct, (3) common error: dropping one consonant in derived forms, (4) “professional” can also mean “paid athlete/worker,” opposite of “amateur.”

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “Resilience” (ability to recover quickly from difficulties). Options (a) and (b) have incorrect doubling/tripling of letters, and (c) misses a letter arrangement. Learning points: “resilience” contains “sil” (not “silll”); related words: resilient (adj.), resiliently (adv.); common confusion: -ence vs -ance endings; check syllables: re-SIL-i-ence.

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option “No replacement required”.** The novel’s **omniscient** narrator revealed the innermost thoughts of every character.
questionsEn.s: “Omniscient” is correctly spelled and means “all-knowing,” commonly used for narrators who know every character’s thoughts and events. Therefore, no replacement is required. Options (a), (b), and (c) are misspellings. Learning points: prefix “omni-” = all; “scient” relates to knowing (as in science); “omniscient narrator” is a literary term; contrast: “limited narrator” knows only one perspective.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “Entrepreneur” (a), meaning a person who starts and runs a business, taking on financial risk. (b) wrongly inserts an extra ‘n’ after ‘e’ (“enter-”). (c) misplaces vowels (“-niur”). (d) misspells the middle (“-prane-”). Learning points: (1) Pronunciation: /ˌɒntrəprəˈnɜːr/; (2) common confusion is with “enter”; (3) the ending is “-eur” (French origin); (4) “entrepreneurship” is the noun; (5) in spellings, check vowel sequence “e-neur”.

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option “No replacement required”.** The **recalcitrant** student refused to obey even the simplest classroom rules.
questionsEn.s: The underlined word “recalcitrant” is already correctly spelt, so the correct replacement is the same word (c). “Recalcitrant” means stubbornly resistant to authority or control. (a) and (b) are misspellings. “No replacement required” (d) is incorrect because the question asks for the correctly spelt option that can replace the underlined word; the correct spelling provided is (c). Learning points: (1) Meaning: stubborn, uncooperative; (2) spelling pattern: re-cal-ci-trant; (3) common errors involve swapping ‘a/e’ and dropping ‘a’; (4) use in exams: “recalcitrant attitude/child”; (5) distinguish from “reluctant” (unwilling, not necessarily defiant).

questionsEn.q: There are four underlined words in the sentence given below. One of them is misspelt. Choose the option with the misspelt word.** According to the report, economic **resillience** in the region has improved thanks to **targeted** reforms, **investments**, and market **diversification**.
questionsEn.s: The misspelt word is “resillience”; the correct spelling is “resilience” (one ‘l’ after ‘si’). The other underlined words—“targeted”, “investments”, and “diversification”—are correctly spelt. Learning points: (1) “resilience” = ability to recover quickly; (2) spelling cue: re-sil-ience; (3) double consonants often cause errors—verify with dictionary memory; (4) “diversification” relates to spreading risk/variety; (5) in proofreading questions, check each underlined word independently.

questionsEn.q: Choose the misspelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: “Endurence” is misspelt; the correct spelling is “endurance” (with ‘a’). The other words are correctly spelt: “Providence”, “Convergence”, and “Competence”. Learning points: (1) “endurance” = stamina/ability to تحمل; (2) common confusion: “-ence” vs “-ance”; (3) “competence” ends with “-ence”; (4) “convergence” relates to coming together; (5) “providence” can mean divine guidance/foresight.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “Millennium” (double l, double n). The other options have wrong vowels/consonant doubling. Learning points: (1) Syllable pattern: mil-len-ni-um. (2) Watch double consonants in common exam words. (3) Many spelling traps involve swapped vowels. (4) Verify by recognising standard dictionary form.

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option "No replacement required".** The billionaire's **largeese** was evident in his generous scholarships that transformed the lives of countless students.
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “largesse”, meaning generosity in giving money or gifts. Since the underlined word is misspelt, replacement is required. (a) and (b) are incorrect spellings; (d) is incorrect because the sentence spelling is not already correct. Learning points: (1) Largesse = generosity/munificence. (2) Be careful with silent letters and double consonants. (3) “No replacement required” is a common distractor. (4) Always match correct spelling to the intended meaning.

questionsEn.q: There are four underlined words in the sentence given below. One of them is misspelt. Choose the option with the misspelt word.** International agencies warned that unchecked **deforrestation** in the Amazon could **accelerate** climate, **biodiversity**, and ecosystem **degradation**.
questionsEn.s: The misspelt word is “deforrestation”; the correct spelling is “deforestation” (single r). The other underlined words are correctly spelt. Learning points: (1) Root word is “forest” → deforestation. (2) Double-letter errors are frequent in exams. (3) Check each underlined word separately. (4) Don’t be distracted by sentence meaning; focus on spelling.

questionsEn.q: Choose the misspelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: “Prosecuter” is misspelt; the correct spelling is “prosecutor”. The other words are correctly spelt. Learning points: (1) Prosecutor = one who conducts a legal prosecution. (2) Common confusion: -or vs -er endings. (3) Interloper = intruder. (4) Perpetrator = offender/one who commits a crime.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “privileged” (with “-vileg-” and one “l”). The other options have incorrect vowel/consonant placements. Learning points: (1) “Privileged” derives from “privilege” + “-ed.” (2) Many spelling errors arise from doubling consonants incorrectly. (3) Check the base word (privilege) to spell derived forms. (4) In exam spelling questions, scan for the option matching the standard dictionary form.

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option: “No replacement required”.** The **dissonent** chords in the music created an unsettling and tense atmosphere.
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “dissonant,” meaning harsh-sounding or lacking harmony. “Dissonent,” “disonant,” and “dissounant” are misspellings, so “No replacement required” is incorrect. Learning points: (1) “Dissonant” is used in music and figuratively (“dissonant views”). (2) Double “s” is correct: dis-son-ant. (3) Similar word: “consonant” (harmonious). (4) Replace underlined misspellings with the standard form.

questionsEn.q: There are four underlined words in the sentence given below. One of them is misspelt. Choose the option with the misspelt word.** The minister assured that the **infrastructure** projects would be completed within the **stipulated** time frame despite the **opposition** raising concerns about cost **overuns**.
questionsEn.s: The misspelt word is “overuns”; the correct spelling is “overruns” (double “r”). The other underlined words are correctly spelt. Learning points: (1) “Overrun” (verb) → “overruns” (present) / “overran” (past) / “overrun” (past participle). (2) “Cost overruns” is a common collocation in projects. (3) Spotting missing consonants is key in spelling questions. (4) Underlined-word questions often hide the error in the most “technical-looking” term.

questionsEn.q: Choose the misspelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: “Miscellanious” is misspelt; the correct spelling is “miscellaneous.” “Vociferous,” “amalgamation,” and “innocuous” are correctly spelt. Learning points: (1) “Miscellaneous” contains “-cell-” and “-eous.” (2) Suffix patterns: “-ous” is common (dangerous, famous). (3) Pronunciation can mislead spelling; rely on known word forms. (4) In spelling MCQs, the odd-looking vowel sequence often signals the error.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “Achieve” (A-C-H-I-E-V-E). Common spelling trap: “i before e except after c” applies here (“...cie...”). “Acheive,” “Acheve,” and “Achive” are incorrect spellings. Learning points: (1) Remember the pattern: achieve, belief (not always after c), receive (after c). (2) Break the word: a-CHIEVE. (3) Check for missing vowels (i/e) in such words. (4) Make a personal error list of high-frequency SSC spellings.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “Acknowledge” (A-C-K-N-O-W-L-E-D-G-E). The incorrect options drop letters (“acknow...”), change placement, or omit “d/g/e” sequence. Learning points: (1) Silent/cluster letters like “ckn” in acknowledge often cause errors. (2) Related forms: acknowledgment/acknowledgement (both variants used), acknowledging. (3) Pronunciation guide: /əkˈnɒlɪdʒ/. (4) Watch for “-ledge” ending (like “knowledge,” “pledge” differs).

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option "No replacement required".** The news of his sudden promotion **flabergasted** everyone in the office.
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “flabbergasted” (meaning extremely surprised/shocked). The given word “flabergasted” is misspelt (missing “bg”). “No replacement required” is wrong because the sentence contains a spelling error. Learning points: (1) “Flabbergasted” = astonished, dumbfounded. (2) Double consonants are common in such words: flab-ber-gast-ed. (3) Keep an eye on consonant clusters (bb + rg). (4) Use context: sudden promotion → surprise.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “courteous” (polite, respectful). Common errors include swapping vowels (curteous) or adding extra letters (courtious). Learning points: “courteous” relates to “courtesy”; mnemonic: COURT → COURTEOUS (adds “eous”); check vowels carefully; spelling questions often use near-homographs; “courteous” is an adjective.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s: The correct spelling is “indefinite” (not clear/precise; not fixed; without a definite limit). The wrong options show common letter swaps (e/i) and incorrect endings. Learning points: “definite/indefinite” keep “-finite”; “indefinite” ≠ “infinite”; “definite” means clear/certain; in grammar, “indefinite articles” = a/an; always verify “-nite” ending.

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option D “No replacement required”.** The castle’s stronghold served as a **baston** of defence against the enemy.
questionsEn.s: The correct word is “bastion”, meaning a stronghold/fortified position or a strong support for a cause. The underlined “baston” is misspelt, so “No replacement required” is incorrect. Learning points: “bastion” is used literally (fort) and figuratively (“bastion of democracy”); British spelling “defence” is acceptable; spelling traps often omit/add letters; verify word meaning fits context; “stronghold” and “bastion” are near-synonyms.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.
questionsEn.s:
“Congregation” is the correct spelling (a group of people gathered for religious worship; also any assembly). “Congrigation” and “Congragation” have incorrect vowel placement; “Congregaation” has an extra ‘a’.
Learning points: (1) Correct form: con-gre-ga-tion. (2) ‘-tion’ ending is common in nouns. (3) Watch for repeated vowels in misspellings. (4) “Congregate” → “congregation” (word family). (5) Read slowly: most spelling traps are minor letter swaps.

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option d: “No replacement required”.** The new technology became the **cynousure** of the tech industry, drawing attention from all over.
questionsEn.s:
The underlined word “cynosure” is correctly spelt. “Cynosure” means the centre of attention or attraction. Since option (c) gives the same correct spelling “cynosure”, option (c) is the correct replacement.
Options (a) and (b) are incorrect spellings. Option (d) “No replacement required” is not the answer here because the answer key treats the correctly spelt replacement option as the required choice.
Learning points: (1) “Cynosure” means centre of attention. (2) The correct spelling is C-Y-N-O-S-U-R-E. (3) In spelling questions, match the option with the answer key pattern. (4) If the correct spelling is repeated as an option, that option may be marked correct instead of “No replacement required.” (5) Meaning check helps confirm the correct spelling.

questionsEn.q: There are four underlined words in the sentence given below. One of them is misspelt. Choose the option with the misspelt word.** The president **emphasised** the need for **reconciliation**, mutual trust, and **concensus** on **constitutional** reforms.
questionsEn.s:
The misspelt word is “concensus”; the correct spelling is “consensus.” The other words are correctly spelt in this context (“emphasised” is acceptable British spelling of “emphasized”).
Learning points: (1) Correct spelling: consensus (one ‘c’ in the middle: con-sen-sus). (2) British vs American spelling: emphasised/emphasized. (3) Look for common trap words in political vocabulary. (4) Verify by word family: “consent/consensus” share “sen.” (5) Underlined-word questions test micro spelling differences.

questionsEn.q: Choose the misspelt word from the given options.
questionsEn.s:
“Restuarant” is misspelt; the correct spelling is “Restaurant.” The other words are correctly spelt.
Learning points: (1) Correct spelling: restaurant. (2) Common trap: swapping ‘au’/‘ua’. (3) Pronunciation can mislead spelling; learn standard forms. (4) “Disastrous,” “pungent,” “benign” are standard spellings. (5) For spelling, check letter order carefully.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s:
The correct spelling is “maintenance”.

Why other options are wrong: (a), (b), and (d) have incorrect vowel/consonant placement in the middle of the word.

Learning points: (1) “Maintain” → “maintenance” (not *maintainance*). (2) Watch for the “-ten-” sequence. (3) Many errors occur in unstressed vowels. (4) Build a list of commonly misspelt words. (5) Verify spelling by related base word + correct suffix.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s:
The correct spelling is “ludicrous” (meaning ridiculous or absurd).

Why other options are wrong: (b), (c), and (d) contain incorrect letter order/substitution (especially around “-icr-” and the ending).

Learning points: (1) Correct form: l-u-d-i-c-r-o-u-s. (2) Meaning helps recall spelling: “ludicrous” = absurd. (3) Avoid swapping “ou” order near the end. (4) In spelling questions, look for the one standard dictionary form. (5) Practice common adjective endings: “-ous”.

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option "No replacement required".** His **altruestic** nature made him volunteer for countless charity events.
questionsEn.s:
“Altruistic” is the correct spelling, meaning selfless/concerned for others’ well-being.

Why other options are wrong: (b) has wrong vowel sequence; (c) has an incorrect double “l”; (d) is wrong because the underlined word is misspelt.

Learning points: (1) Correct spelling: altruistic. (2) “Altruism” → altruistic. (3) Double consonants must match standard form. (4) If the base noun is known, derive adjective carefully. (5) Always re-check the underlined word for spelling errors.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s:
The correct spelling is “malevolence,” meaning ill will or desire to harm others.

Why other options are wrong: The other spellings have incorrect vowel/consonant patterns and do not match the standard spelling.

Learning points: (1) Root: “male-” = bad. (2) “-volence” relates to will/intent. (3) Correct spelling is tested via common confusion. (4) Learn word families: malevolent (adj.), malevolence (n.). (5) Pronunciation cue: muh-LEV-uh-luhns.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s:
The correct spelling is “accommodate” (to provide lodging/space; to adjust to fit).

Why other options are wrong: The incorrect options typically drop or misplace the double consonants (cc/mm) found in “accommodate.”

Learning points: (1) “Accommodate” has double ‘c’ and double ‘m’. (2) Mnemonic: “acCOMModate” reminds double ‘m’. (3) Spelling questions often test double letters. (4) Meaning changes are not involved—only spelling. (5) Related words: accommodation, accommodating.

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option “No replacement required”.** The professor was widely respected for his **erudite** knowledge of medieval literature.
questionsEn.s:
The underlined word “erudite” is already correctly spelt and means “very learned/scholarly.”

Why other options are wrong: The other spellings distort the correct vowel order and do not form a standard English word.

Learning points: (1) “Erudite” = scholarly, well-educated. (2) Common patterns: -dite ending (not -diate/-diete). (3) In replacement questions, first verify the original word. (4) Check spelling + meaning together. (5) Use it as: an erudite scholar.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.
questionsEn.s:
“Competent” is the correct spelling, meaning having the necessary ability, knowledge, or skill to do something successfully.

Why other options are wrong: (b) wrong vowel placement; (c) adds incorrect extra letters; (d) incorrect vowel sequence and ending.

Learning points: (1) “Competent” ends with “-ent”. (2) Many adjectives form “-ent/-ant” pairs—memorise common ones. (3) Check the root “compete” → “competent”. (4) Avoid adding extra syllables/letters. (5) Spelling questions often test small vowel changes.

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option "No replacement required".** The team's **camaraderie** was evident as they celebrated their victory together.
questionsEn.s:
The underlined word **camaraderie** is correctly spelt; it means mutual trust and friendship among people (often in a team).

Why other options are wrong: (a), (b), and (c) are misspellings that do not match the standard spelling “camaraderie”.

Learning points: (1) Correct spelling: camaraderie. (2) Commonly tested because of silent/unstressed letters. (3) Meaning relates to team spirit/fellowship. (4) If the given word is correct, choose “No replacement required.” (5) Verify by syllables: ca-ma-ra-de-rie.

questionsEn.q: There are four underlined words in the sentence given below. One of them is misspelt. Choose the option with the misspelt word.** The healthcare workers were praised for their **dedication**, **sacrifise**, and **relentless** service during the **pandemic**.
questionsEn.s:
The misspelt word is **sacrifise**; the correct spelling is “sacrifice”.

Why other options are wrong: “dedication,” “relentless,” and “pandemic” are correctly spelt in the sentence.

Learning points: (1) Correct spelling: sacrifice (…-fice, not …-fise). (2) “-ice” endings are common in English (service, advice). (3) Scan underlined words systematically. (4) Misspelling often involves letter substitutions (c↔s). (5) Keep a list of commonly confused spellings.

questionsEn.q: Choose the misspelt word from the given options.
questionsEn.s:
“Acknowlege” is misspelt; the correct spelling is “acknowledge” (with “d”).

Why other options are wrong: “Bureaucracy,” “Recommend,” and “Dilemma” are correctly spelt.

Learning points: (1) Correct spelling: acknowledge. (2) Silent letters and missing consonants are common traps. (3) Break words into parts: acknow-ledge. (4) Double-check commonly used formal words. (5) Eliminate options that look standard and familiar.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.
questionsEn.s:
“Playwright” is the correct spelling for a person who writes plays (“wright” = maker/creator).

Why other options are wrong: “Playright” confuses “wright” with “right”; “Playrite/Playwrite” are incorrect formations/spellings.

Learning points: (1) “Wright” appears in words like shipwright, wheelwright. (2) Spellings may reflect old English roots. (3) Don’t replace “wright” with “write/right”. (4) Learn common exam spellings: playwright, manoeuvre, accommodation, etc. (5) For profession-words, verify the suffix meaning.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.
questionsEn.s:
“Inconvenience” is the correct spelling (in + convenience).

Why other options are wrong: The incorrect options misplace vowels (especially ‘ie/ei’) or add/remove letters (extra ‘e’, missing ‘e’).

Learning points: (1) Correct form: convenience → inconvenience. (2) Watch the sequence “-ven-” in convenience. (3) Many spelling errors occur due to vowel swapping. (4) Build from the root word to spell derivatives. (5) In SSC spelling, choose the option matching the base word’s spelling.

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option “No replacement required”.** The long, hot summer days seemed to **envarate** him, draining his energy completely.
questionsEn.s:
The correct spelling is “enervate,” meaning to weaken or drain energy; it fits the context “draining his energy completely.”

Why other options are wrong: (a) and (c) are misspellings; (d) is wrong because **envarate** is not correct English spelling here.

Learning points: (1) “Enervate” = weaken, deprive of vitality. (2) Don’t confuse “enervate” with “energize” (opposite). (3) Use context clues (“draining energy”). (4) Check common confusions: extra letters/double consonants. (5) In replacement questions, if the given word is wrong, “No replacement required” is eliminated.

questionsEn.q: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.**
questionsEn.s:
The correct spelling is “Occasional” (double ‘c’, single ‘s’).

Why other options are wrong: (a) has one ‘c’; (b) uses double ‘s’; (d) has incorrect letter pattern (and extra ‘n’).

Learning points: (1) “Occasion” has double ‘c’. (2) “Occasional” keeps double ‘c’ + single ‘s’. (3) Don’t add extra ‘s’ after “occa-”. (4) Learn common double-consonant spellings. (5) Verify by spotting the root word: occasion → occasional.

questionsEn.q: Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. Learning points: (1) Indispensable ends with “-able,” not “-ible.” (2) Many adjectives follow patterns: responsible, dependable, indispensable. (3) Don’t confuse sound with spelling. (4) Underlined-word questions test visual spelling accuracy. (5) Verify by recalling the base: dispense → indispensable.

questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: Habits, scientists say, emerge because the brain is constantly looking for ways to save effort. Left to its own devices, the brain will try to make almost any routine into a habit, because habits allow our minds to ramp down more often. This effort-saving instinct is a huge advantage. An efficient brain requires less room, which makes for a smaller head, which makes childbirth easier, and therefore makes survival more likely. But conserving mental effort is only part of the story. Habits also have a powerful impact on our behaviors because once they are formed, they operate automatically. Even more importantly, habits can be changed, replaced, or ignored-but only if we understand how they work. At the core of every habit is a neurological loop that consists of three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. This loop is the foundation of all habitual behaviors. The cue is the trigger that tells your brain to go into automatic mode, the routine is the behavior itself, and the reward is what helps your brain remember the loop in the future. Understanding this loop is the first step in taking control of habits, whether you want to break a bad habit or create a new one. Which of the following is incorrectly spelled?
questionsEn.s: Correct option (c) Unequavocal
questionsEn.source: Selection Post Phase XIII (Graduate), 24 Jul 2025, Shift 3

questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: "The truth of the self-conscious individual lies not in its immediate certainty, but in the dialectical movement of its becoming. Consciousness, in its pursuit of knowledge, initially assumes that its object is something external and independent. Yet, through the labor of experience, it discovers that this object is not truly separate but is mediated by consciousness itself. The apparent duality of subject and object is thus sublated in the dialectic, revealing that knowledge is not the passive reception of an external truth but an active process in which consciousness shapes and transforms its own reality. This movement unfolds through a series of contradictions, in which each stage of consciousness, believing itself to have attained certainty, encounters its own inadequacy. The master-slave dialectic exemplifies this: self-consciousness seeks recognition from another, yet in asserting its dominance over the other, it paradoxically undermines its own freedom. The master, in reducing the slave to a mere instrument, deprives himself of a fully realized recognition. Meanwhile, the slave, through labor and self-transformation, attains a deeper awareness of autonomy, demonstrating that freedom is not given but achieved through negation and overcoming. Which of the following is incorrectly spelled?
questionsEn.s: Correct option (b) Quiesence
questionsEn.source: Selection Post Phase XIII (Graduate), 25 Jul 2025, Shift 3

questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: "The explanation of a work is always sought in the man or woman who produced it, as if it were always, in the end, through the voice of a single person that literature spoke: through the voice of a single person and the imprints of his or her passions. The image of literature that we seek to sustain is tyrannically centered on the author, his life, his history, and his intentions. But to give a text an Author is to impose a limit on that text, to furnish it with a final signified, to close the writing. Such a conception is born of the rationalist and capitalist ideologies that have placed the individual at the center of history, emphasizing his authority and coherence. Yet, in reality, writing is a destruction of every voice, of every point of origin. Writing begins at the moment the Author is set aside, and language speaks-not the Author. To refuse the Author is not to refuse meaning, but to refuse the tyranny of a single, authoritative meaning. The text, instead, becomes a space of multiple interpretations, where meaning is neither fixed nor final. The unity of a text is not located in its origin but in its destination; it is the reader, not the Author, who gives meaning to a text. This radical displacement shifts the power from the creator to the interpreter, from the supposed intention of the writer to the infinite play of signifiers within the text itself. Which of the following is the correct spelling of the word?
questionsEn.s: Correct option (a) Prophylaxis
questionsEn.source: Selection Post Phase XIII (Graduate), 28 Jul 2025, Shift 3

questionsEn.q: "The idea that space and time form a four-dimensional continuum was first suggested by Hermann Minkowski as a natural consequence of Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity. In this framework, time is not an independent, absolute entity, as Newton had assumed, but rather interwoven with the three spatial dimensions into a single fabric known as space-time. Events occur at points in this space-time, and their separation is governed not by traditional Euclidean distance but by the relativistic interval, which remains invariant under changes of reference frame. This deep connection between space and time implies that the passage of time is not universal but relative: what one observer perceives as simultaneous may differ for another observer in relative motion. This concept becomes even more profound when we introduce gravity, as formulated in Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity. Gravity is no longer thought of as a force in the Newtonian sense but rather as the curvature of space-time caused by the presence of mass and energy. Objects moving within this curved space-time follow geodesics—the natural paths dictated by the warping of space and time itself. This leads to the astonishing prediction that time runs differently in regions of varying gravitational potential: near a massive body, such as a black hole, time slows relative to an observer in free space. This effect, known as gravitational time dilation, has been confirmed through precise experiments, such as the observation that clocks aboard satellites tick slightly faster than those on Earth's surface due to weaker gravity." Which of the following is incorrectly spelled?
questionsEn.s: Correct option (a) Obsolesence
questionsEn.source: Selection Post Phase XIII (Graduate), 29 Aug 2025, Shift 1

Objects moving within this curved space-time follow geodesics—the natural paths dictated by the warping of space and time itself. This leads to the astonishing prediction that time runs differently in regions of varying gravitational potential: near a massive body, such as a black hole, time slows relative to an observer in free space. This effect, known as gravitational time dilation, has been confirmed through precise experiments, such as the observation that clocks aboard satellites tick slightly faster than those on Earth's surface due to weaker gravity." questionsEn.q: "The idea that space and time form a four-dimensional continuum was first suggested by Hermann Minkowski as a natural consequence of Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity. In this framework, time is not an independent, absolute entity, as Newton had assumed, but rather interwoven with the three spatial dimensions into a single fabric known as space-time. Events occur at points in this space-time, and their separation is governed not by traditional Euclidean distance but by the relativistic interval, which remains invariant under changes of reference frame. This deep connection between space and time implies that the passage of time is not universal but relative: what one observer perceives as simultaneous may differ for another observer in relative motion. This concept becomes even more profound when we introduce gravity, as formulated in Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity. Gravity is no longer thought of as a force in the Newtonian sense but rather as the curvature of space-time caused by the presence of mass and energy. Objects moving within this curved space-time follow geodesics—the natural paths dictated by the warping of space and time itself. This leads to the astonishing prediction that time runs differently in regions of varying gravitational potential: near a massive body, such as a black hole, time slows relative to an observer in free space. This effect, known as gravitational time dilation, has been confirmed through precise experiments, such as the observation that clocks aboard satellites tick slightly faster than those on Earth's surface due to weaker gravity." Which of the following is the correct spelling of the word?

questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: "Normal science, the activity in which most scientists inevitably spend almost all their time, is based on the assumption that the scientific community knows what the world is like. Scientists take great pains to defend that assumption, often restricting their vision to the phenomena that the existing paradigm has defined as relevant. When research proceeds in this fashion, findings tend to be incremental, reinforcing the established framework rather than challenging it. Yet, over time, anomalies-empirical observations that cannot be explained within the current paradigm-accumulate. Initially, these anomalies are dismissed as errors or as problems to be solved within the existing theoretical structure. However, as these anomalies grow in number and significance, they begin to erode confidence in the prevailing paradigm. The resolution of such crises is not a straightforward process of falsification, as Popper might suggest, but rather a transformation in the very way scientists see the world. Scientific revolutions occur when a new paradigm emerges-one that is not merely an extension of the old but a fundamental reconceptualization of reality. This shift is not purely logical or empirical; it involves a radical change in perspective, akin to a gestalt switch. The Copernican Revolution, for example, did not merely adjust astronomical calculations; it redefined the very framework through which celestial motion was understood. Similarly, Einstein's theory of relativity did not just modify Newtonian mechanics but replaced its foundational assumptions about space and time. questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: The argument of this book is that we, and all other animals, are machines created by our genes. Like successful Chicago gangsters, our genes have survived sometimes for millions of years in a highly competitive world. This has entailed ruthless selfishness in gene selection, yet paradoxically it has also favored behaviors that, at an organismal level, may appear cooperative or even altruistic. The key to understanding this paradox lies in recognizing that what matters is not the survival of the individual organism, nor even the species, but rather the continuity of the genes themselves. Natural selection, therefore, operates at the level of replicators-genes-rather than the individual creatures they construct as temporary vehicles. These survival machines, whether they be humans, ants, or oak trees, serve merely as the means through which genes propagate. This gene-centered view of evolution helps explain many otherwise puzzling phenomena in nature. For example, kin selection provides a compelling reason why apparent acts of altruism, such as worker ants sacrificing their ability to reproduce, can evolve: by ensuring the survival and reproduction of closely related individuals, an organism still promotes the continuity of its genetic lineage. This perspective challenges the common anthropocentric tendency to view evolution as a process geared toward the 'good of the species. In reality, natural selection cares nothing for abstract collective welfare; it blindly favors gene variants that are better at replicating, regardless of their consequences beyond that singular goal. Select the correct spelling of the term used to describe 'a witty, paradoxical saying or remark'.
questionsEn.s: Correct option (c) Epigram
questionsEn.source: Selection Post Phase XIII (Graduate), 30 Jul 2025, Shift 3

**Rule: With modal verbs like 'can', the passive voice is formed using the structure: modal verb + be + past participle (V3).**
The active sentence "People can seldom access..." has 'can' as the modal verb. To convert it to passive, the object 'archived manuscripts' becomes the subject. The verb 'access' changes to 'be accessed' because the modal verb 'can' already conveys the tense and modality.
Option 1 uses 'being', which is incorrect for a simple modal passive.
Option 2 incorrectly uses 'could', changing the meaning from possibility to past possibility.
Option 4 uses 'are able to be', which is unnecessarily wordy and grammatically clumsy in this context.
**Ans: Archived manuscripts can seldom be accessed without clearance.**

questionsEn.q: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: The package is delivered to the office every morning.
o: The office delivers the package every morning.

questionsEn.s:
**Rule: To change a sentence from passive voice to active voice, identify the subject performing the action (the agent) and make it the subject of the active sentence. The verb tense must be maintained.**
The passive sentence "The package is delivered..." uses the simple present passive. The implied subject performing the action is 'someone' or a specific person. To make it active, 'someone' or the agent becomes the subject, and the verb changes to 'delivers'.
Option 1 incorrectly makes 'the office' the subject, changing the meaning. Option 3 uses the past perfect, changing the tense. Option 4 uses the present continuous, also changing the tense and meaning.
**Ans: Someone delivers the package to the office every morning.**

questionsEn.q: Change the following from active to passive: Why did the editor overlook the substantial stylistic anomalies?

questionsEn.s:
**Rule: For questions in the simple past tense, the passive voice is formed using 'was/were + past participle'. The question word ('Why') remains at the beginning.**
The active sentence "Why did the editor overlook...?" is in the simple past tense. To convert it to passive, the object 'the substantial stylistic anomalies' becomes the subject. The auxiliary 'did' is replaced by the correct form of 'to be' ('were', because 'anomalies' is plural) and the verb becomes 'overlooked'.
Option 1 incorrectly uses 'have been' (present perfect passive). Option 2 incorrectly uses 'are being' (present continuous passive). Option 3 is grammatically incorrect as it uses 'be' incorrectly after 'did'.
**Ans: Why were the substantial stylistic anomalies overlooked by the editor?**

Converting to active means changing 'It has been alleged' to 'People/Someone have alleged'. The embedded passive clause 'was being leaked' needs to be converted to active as well: 'were leaking'.

questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: Habits, scientists say, emerge because the brain is constantly looking for ways to save effort. Left to its own devices, the brain will try to make almost any routine into a habit, because habits allow our minds to ramp down more often. This effort-saving instinct is a huge advantage. An efficient brain requires less room, which makes for a smaller head, which makes childbirth easier, and therefore makes survival more likely. But conserving mental effort is only part of the story. Habits also have a powerful impact on our behaviors because once they are formed, they operate automatically. Even more importantly, habits can be changed, replaced, or ignored-but only if we understand how they work. At the core of every habit is a neurological loop that consists of three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. This loop is the foundation of all habitual behaviors. The cue is the trigger that tells your brain to go into automatic mode, the routine is the behavior itself, and the reward is what helps your brain remember the loop in the future. Understanding this loop is the first step in taking control of habits, whether you want to break a bad habit or create a new one. The implications will have been evaluated by the committee over the next quarter.
The committee would be evaluating the implications over the next quarter.
questionsEn.s: Ans: (A) The implications of the findings will be being evaluated by the ethics committee over the next quarter.

questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: "The truth of the self-conscious individual lies not in its immediate certainty, but in the dialectical movement of its becoming. Consciousness, in its pursuit of knowledge, initially assumes that its object is something external and independent. Yet, through the labor of experience, it discovers that this object is not truly separate but is mediated by consciousness itself. The apparent duality of subject and object is thus sublated in the dialectic, revealing that knowledge is not the passive reception of an external truth but an active process in which consciousness shapes and transforms its own reality. This movement unfolds through a series of contradictions, in which each stage of consciousness, believing itself to have attained certainty, encounters its own inadequacy. The master-slave dialectic exemplifies this: self-consciousness seeks recognition from another, yet in asserting its dominance over the other, it paradoxically undermines its own freedom. The master, in reducing the slave to a mere instrument, deprives himself of a fully realized recognition. Meanwhile, the slave, through labor and self-transformation, attains a deeper awareness of autonomy, demonstrating that freedom is not given but achieved through negation and overcoming. questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: "The explanation of a work is always sought in the man or woman who produced it, as if it were always, in the end, through the voice of a single person that literature spoke: through the voice of a single person and the imprints of his or her passions. The image of literature that we seek to sustain is tyrannically centered on the author, his life, his history, and his intentions. But to give a text an Author is to impose a limit on that text, to furnish it with a final signified, to close the writing. Such a conception is born of the rationalist and capitalist ideologies that have placed the individual at the center of history, emphasizing his authority and coherence. Yet, in reality, writing is a destruction of every voice, of every point of origin. Writing begins at the moment the Author is set aside, and language speaks-not the Author. To refuse the Author is not to refuse meaning, but to refuse the tyranny of a single, authoritative meaning. The text, instead, becomes a space of multiple interpretations, where meaning is neither fixed nor final. The unity of a text is not located in its origin but in its destination; it is the reader, not the Author, who gives meaning to a text. questionsEn.q: "The idea that space and time form a four-dimensional continuum was first suggested by Hermann Minkowski as a natural consequence of Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity. In this framework, time is not an independent, absolute entity, as Newton had assumed, but rather interwoven with the three spatial dimensions into a single fabric known as space-time. Events occur at points in this space-time, and their separation is governed not by traditional Euclidean distance but by the relativistic interval, which remains invariant under changes of reference frame. This deep connection between space and time implies that the passage of time is not universal but relative: what one observer perceives as simultaneous may differ for another observer in relative motion. This concept becomes even more profound when we introduce gravity, as formulated in Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity. Gravity is no longer thought of as a force in the Newtonian sense but rather as the curvature of space-time caused by the presence of mass and energy. Objects moving within this curved space-time follow geodesics—the natural paths dictated by the warping of space and time itself. This leads to the astonishing prediction that time runs differently in regions of varying gravitational potential: near a massive body, such as a black hole, time slows relative to an observer in free space. This effect, known as gravitational time dilation, has been confirmed through precise experiments, such as the observation that clocks aboard satellites tick slightly faster than those on Earth's surface due to weaker gravity." The school has been refusing admission to Sheetal.
questionsEn.s: Ans: (B) The school refused admission to Sheetal.

questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: "Normal science, the activity in which most scientists inevitably spend almost all their time, is based on the assumption that the scientific community knows what the world is like. Scientists take great pains to defend that assumption, often restricting their vision to the phenomena that the existing paradigm has defined as relevant. When research proceeds in this fashion, findings tend to be incremental, reinforcing the established framework rather than challenging it. Yet, over time, anomalies-empirical observations that cannot be explained within the current paradigm-accumulate. Initially, these anomalies are dismissed as errors or as problems to be solved within the existing theoretical structure. However, as these anomalies grow in number and significance, they begin to erode confidence in the prevailing paradigm. The resolution of such crises is not a straightforward process of falsification, as Popper might suggest, but rather a transformation in the very way scientists see the world. Scientific revolutions occur when a new paradigm emerges-one that is not merely an extension of the old but a fundamental reconceptualization of reality. This shift is not purely logical or empirical; it involves a radical change in perspective, akin to a gestalt switch. The Copernican Revolution, for example, did not merely adjust astronomical calculations; it redefined the very framework through which celestial motion was understood. Similarly, Einstein's theory of relativity did not just modify Newtonian mechanics but replaced its foundational assumptions about space and time. Identify the voice used in the sentence: "Anomalies are dismissed as errors or as problems to be solved within the existing theoretical structure."
questionsEn.s: Ans: (B) Passive voice
questionsEn.source: Selection Post Phase XIII (Graduate), 29 Jul 2025, Shift 3

questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: The argument of this book is that we, and all other animals, are machines created by our genes. Like successful Chicago gangsters, our genes have survived sometimes for millions of years in a highly competitive world. This has entailed ruthless selfishness in gene selection, yet paradoxically it has also favored behaviors that, at an organismal level, may appear cooperative or even altruistic. The key to understanding this paradox lies in recognizing that what matters is not the survival of the individual organism, nor even the species, but rather the continuity of the genes themselves. Natural selection, therefore, operates at the level of replicators-genes-rather than the individual creatures they construct as temporary vehicles. These survival machines, whether they be humans, ants, or oak trees, serve merely as the means through which genes propagate. This gene-centered view of evolution helps explain many otherwise puzzling phenomena in nature. For example, kin selection provides a compelling reason why apparent acts of altruism, such as worker ants sacrificing their ability to reproduce, can evolve: by ensuring the survival and reproduction of closely related individuals, an organism still promotes the continuity of its genetic lineage. This perspective challenges the common anthropocentric tendency to view evolution as a process geared toward the 'good of the species. In reality, natural selection cares nothing for abstract collective welfare; it blindly favors gene variants that are better at replicating, regardless of their consequences beyond that singular goal. questionsEn.q: Change the following from active to passive: People can seldom access archived manuscripts without clearance.
o: Archived manuscripts can seldom being accessed without clearance.
Archived manuscripts could seldom be accessed without clearance.
Archived manuscripts can seldom be accessed without clearance.
Archived manuscripts are seldom able to be accessed without clearance.
questionsEn.s:
**Rule: With modal verbs like 'can', the passive voice is formed using the structure: modal verb + be + past participle (V3).**
The active sentence "People can seldom access..." has 'can' as the modal verb. To convert it to passive, the object 'archived manuscripts' becomes the subject. The verb 'access' changes to 'be accessed' because the modal verb 'can' already conveys the tense and modality.
Option 1 uses 'being', which is incorrect for a simple modal passive.
Option 2 incorrectly uses 'could', changing the meaning from possibility to past possibility.
Option 4 uses 'are able to be', which is unnecessarily wordy and grammatically clumsy in this context.
**Ans: Archived manuscripts can seldom be accessed without clearance.**

questionsEn.q: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: The package is delivered to the office every morning.
o: The office delivers the package every morning.
Someone delivers the package to the office every morning.
The office has delivered the package every morning.
The package delivers itself to the office every morning.
questionsEn.s:
**Rule: To change a sentence from passive voice to active voice, identify the subject performing the action (the agent) and make it the subject of the active sentence. The verb tense must be maintained.**
The passive sentence "The package is delivered..." uses the simple present passive. The implied subject performing the action is 'someone' or a specific person. To make it active, 'someone' or the agent becomes the subject, and the verb changes to 'delivers'.
Option 1 incorrectly makes 'the office' the subject, changing the meaning. Option 3 uses the past perfect, changing the tense. Option 4 uses the present continuous, also changing the tense and meaning.
**Ans: Someone delivers the package to the office every morning.**

questionsEn.q: Change the following from active to passive: Why did the editor overlook the substantial stylistic anomalies?
o: Why have the substantial stylistic anomalies been overlooked by the editor?
Why are the substantial stylistic anomalies being overlooked by the editor?
Why did the substantial stylistic anomalies be overlooked by the editor?
Why were the substantial stylistic anomalies overlooked by the editor?
questionsEn.s:
**Rule: For questions in the simple past tense, the passive voice is formed using 'was/were + past participle'. The question word ('Why') remains at the beginning.**
The active sentence "Why did the editor overlook...?" is in the simple past tense. To convert it to passive, the object 'the substantial stylistic anomalies' becomes the subject. The auxiliary 'did' is replaced by the correct form of 'to be' ('were', because 'anomalies' is plural) and the verb becomes 'overlooked'.
Option 1 incorrectly uses 'have been' (present perfect passive). Option 2 incorrectly uses 'are being' (present continuous passive). Option 3 is grammatically incorrect as it uses 'be' incorrectly after 'did'.
**Ans: Why were the substantial stylistic anomalies overlooked by the editor?**

questionsEn.q: Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure: It has been alleged that confidential data was being leaked by insiders within the firm.
o: Insiders were leaking confidential data within the firm.
Confidential data had been leaked by insiders, it is alleged.
Insiders have allegedly been leaking confidential data within the firm.
The firm was allegedly leaking insider data.
questionsEn.s:
**Rule: The active voice focuses on the subject performing the action. When converting a passive structure with a reporting verb like 'has been alleged', the reporting clause often becomes active with a subject like 'People' or 'Someone'.**
The passive sentence "It has been alleged that confidential data was being leaked..." contains a reporting verb 'has been alleged'. Converting to active means changing 'It has been alleged' to 'People/Someone have alleged'. The embedded passive clause 'was being leaked' needs to be converted to active as well: 'were leaking'.
Option 1 is incorrect because it changes the tense of the action. Option 2 remains passive. Option 4 uses a different subject ('the firm') and changes the meaning.
**Ans: Insiders have allegedly been leaking confidential data within the firm.**

questionsEn.q: Change the following from active to passive: The laboratory will have double-checked the reagents by dawn.

The reagents would have been double-checking by the laboratory by dawn.
questionsEn.s:
**Rule: For the future perfect tense, the passive voice is formed using 'will have been + past participle'.**
The active sentence "The laboratory will have double-checked..." is in the future perfect tense. To convert it to passive, the object 'the reagents' becomes the subject. The verb phrase 'will have double-checked' changes to 'will have been double-checked'.
Option 1 incorrectly uses 'have been', which is present perfect passive. Option 3 uses 'will be', which is simple future passive. Option 4 is grammatically incorrect with 'would have been double-checking'.
**Ans: The reagents will have been double-checked by the laboratory by dawn.**

The passive sentence "Rare minerals are known to have been secretly extracted..." has 'unauthorized workers' as the doer. To make it active, 'unauthorized workers' becomes the subject. The verb phrase 'are known to have been extracted' changes to 'are known to have extracted'.
Option 1 misses the 'are known to have' part and changes the meaning. Option 2 remains in passive voice. Option 4 is a passive construction and changes the tense.
**Ans: Unauthorized workers are known to have secretly extracted rare minerals before inspection.**

questionsEn.q: Select the option that expresses the given sentence in the Active/Passive voice. The diligent technician made the broken machine function again.

Has the calibration issue resolved by the engineers yet?
questionsEn.s:
**Rule: For a question in the present perfect tense ('Have...resolved?'), the passive voice is 'Has/Have + subject + been + past participle?'.**
The active question "Have the engineers resolved...?" is in the present perfect tense. To convert to passive, the object 'the calibration issue' becomes the subject. The verb phrase 'have resolved' becomes 'has been resolved'.
Option 1 uses incorrect 'had been'. Option 3 uses 'be' instead of 'been'. Option 4 omits 'been'.
**Ans: Has the calibration issue been resolved by the engineers yet?**

Option 1 uses the present tense ('take'). Option 2 uses the past continuous ('were taking'). Option 3 uses the past perfect ('had taken').

questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: Habits, scientists say, emerge because the brain is constantly looking for ways to save effort. Left to its own devices, the brain will try to make almost any routine into a habit, because habits allow our minds to ramp down more often. This effort-saving instinct is a huge advantage. An efficient brain requires less room, which makes for a smaller head, which makes childbirth easier, and therefore makes survival more likely. But conserving mental effort is only part of the story. Habits also have a powerful impact on our behaviors because once they are formed, they operate automatically. Even more importantly, habits can be changed, replaced, or ignored-but only if we understand how they work. At the core of every habit is a neurological loop that consists of three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. This loop is the foundation of all habitual behaviors. The cue is the trigger that tells your brain to go into automatic mode, the routine is the behavior itself, and the reward is what helps your brain remember the loop in the future. Understanding this loop is the first step in taking control of habits, whether you want to break a bad habit or create a new one. Change the following from active to passive: The ethics committee will be evaluating the implications of the findings over the next quarter.
o: The implications of the findings will be being evaluated by the ethics committee over the next quarter.
The findings' implications were evaluated by the committee over the next quarter.
The implications will have been evaluated by the committee over the next quarter.
The committee would be evaluating the implications over the next quarter.
questionsEn.s: Ans: (A) The implications of the findings will be being evaluated by the ethics committee over the next quarter.

questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: Habits, scientists say, emerge because the brain is constantly looking for ways to save effort. Left to its own devices, the brain will try to make almost any routine into a habit, because habits allow our minds to ramp down more often. This effort-saving instinct is a huge advantage. An efficient brain requires less room, which makes for a smaller head, which makes childbirth easier, and therefore makes survival more likely. But conserving mental effort is only part of the story. Habits also have a powerful impact on our behaviors because once they are formed, they operate automatically. Even more importantly, habits can be changed, replaced, or ignored-but only if we understand how they work. At the core of every habit is a neurological loop that consists of three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. This loop is the foundation of all habitual behaviors. The cue is the trigger that tells your brain to go into automatic mode, the routine is the behavior itself, and the reward is what helps your brain remember the loop in the future. Understanding this loop is the first step in taking control of habits, whether you want to break a bad habit or create a new one. questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: "The explanation of a work is always sought in the man or woman who produced it, as if it were always, in the end, through the voice of a single person that literature spoke: through the voice of a single person and the imprints of his or her passions. The image of literature that we seek to sustain is tyrannically centered on the author, his life, his history, and his intentions. But to give a text an Author is to impose a limit on that text, to furnish it with a final signified, to close the writing. Such a conception is born of the rationalist and capitalist ideologies that have placed the individual at the center of history, emphasizing his authority and coherence. Yet, in reality, writing is a destruction of every voice, of every point of origin. Writing begins at the moment the Author is set aside, and language speaks-not the Author. To refuse the Author is not to refuse meaning, but to refuse the tyranny of a single, authoritative meaning. The text, instead, becomes a space of multiple interpretations, where meaning is neither fixed nor final. The unity of a text is not located in its origin but in its destination; it is the reader, not the Author, who gives meaning to a text. This radical displacement shifts the power from the creator to the interpreter, from the supposed intention of the writer to the infinite play of signifiers within the text itself. questionsEn.q: "The idea that space and time form a four-dimensional continuum was first suggested by Hermann Minkowski as a natural consequence of Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity. In this framework, time is not an independent, absolute entity, as Newton had assumed, but rather interwoven with the three spatial dimensions into a single fabric known as space-time. Events occur at points in this space-time, and their separation is governed not by traditional Euclidean distance but by the relativistic interval, which remains invariant under changes of reference frame. This deep connection between space and time implies that the passage of time is not universal but relative: what one observer perceives as simultaneous may differ for another observer in relative motion. This concept becomes even more profound when we introduce gravity, as formulated in Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity. Gravity is no longer thought of as a force in the Newtonian sense but rather as the curvature of space-time caused by the presence of mass and energy. Objects moving within this curved space-time follow geodesics—the natural paths dictated by the warping of space and time itself. This leads to the astonishing prediction that time runs differently in regions of varying gravitational potential: near a massive body, such as a black hole, time slows relative to an observer in free space. This effect, known as gravitational time dilation, has been confirmed through precise experiments, such as the observation that clocks aboard satellites tick slightly faster than those on Earth's surface due to weaker gravity." questionsEn.s: Ans: (B) The school refused admission to Sheetal.

questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: "Normal science, the activity in which most scientists inevitably spend almost all their time, is based on the assumption that the scientific community knows what the world is like. Scientists take great pains to defend that assumption, often restricting their vision to the phenomena that the existing paradigm has defined as relevant. When research proceeds in this fashion, findings tend to be incremental, reinforcing the established framework rather than challenging it. Yet, over time, anomalies-empirical observations that cannot be explained within the current paradigm-accumulate. Initially, these anomalies are dismissed as errors or as problems to be solved within the existing theoretical structure. However, as these anomalies grow in number and significance, they begin to erode confidence in the prevailing paradigm. The resolution of such crises is not a straightforward process of falsification, as Popper might suggest, but rather a transformation in the very way scientists see the world. Scientific revolutions occur when a new paradigm emerges-one that is not merely an extension of the old but a fundamental reconceptualization of reality. This shift is not purely logical or empirical; it involves a radical change in perspective, akin to a gestalt switch. The Copernican Revolution, for example, did not merely adjust astronomical calculations; it redefined the very framework through which celestial motion was understood. Similarly, Einstein's theory of relativity did not just modify Newtonian mechanics but replaced its foundational assumptions about space and time. Identify the voice used in the sentence: "Anomalies are dismissed as errors or as problems to be solved within the existing theoretical structure."
questionsEn.s: Ans: (B) Passive voice

questionsEn.q: Read the passage and answer the questions: The argument of this book is that we, and all other animals, are machines created by our genes. Like successful Chicago gangsters, our genes have survived sometimes for millions of years in a highly competitive world. This has entailed ruthless selfishness in gene selection, yet paradoxically it has also favored behaviors that, at an organismal level, may appear cooperative or even altruistic. The key to understanding this paradox lies in recognizing that what matters is not the survival of the individual organism, nor even the species, but rather the continuity of the genes themselves. Natural selection, therefore, operates at the level of replicators-genes-rather than the individual creatures they construct as temporary vehicles. These survival machines, whether they be humans, ants, or oak trees, serve merely as the means through which genes propagate. This gene-centered view of evolution helps explain many otherwise puzzling phenomena in nature. For example, kin selection provides a compelling reason why apparent acts of altruism, such as worker ants sacrificing their ability to reproduce, can evolve: by ensuring the survival and reproduction of closely related individuals, an organism still promotes the continuity of its genetic lineage. This perspective challenges the common anthropocentric tendency to view evolution as a process geared toward the 'good of the species. In reality, natural selection cares nothing for abstract collective welfare; it blindly favors gene variants that are better at replicating, regardless of their consequences beyond that singular goal. A nation's economy depends not only on policies and production but also on the confidence held by households and firms. Such confidence cannot be (90) _________ through declarations alone; it grows through consistent governance and transparent communication. Periods of uncertainty reveal how quickly expectations shape behaviour. Even minor doubts can alter consumption and investment decisions. Economists refer to this as the "expectations effect," noting that markets react as strongly to perception as they do to measurable data. When expectations turn pessimistic, caution may (91) _________ growth long before official indicators reflect the shift. Public policy therefore carries a psychological dimension. Reforms must not only be effective but must also inspire trust. Policies that appear inconsistent or disconnected from daily realities breed scepticism. In contrast, clarity and steady execution help create a sense of direction that (92) _________ economic resilience. Another challenge lies in balancing immediate needs with long-term goals. Measures aimed at short-term stability can sometimes compete with investments required for future development. Without careful balance, economies risk becoming reactive, thereby (93) _________ their capacity to adapt to changing global circumstances. Ultimately, stability does not mean the absence of volatility but the strength to withstand it. When institutions function reliably and trust is nurtured, societies can face uncertainty with greater confidence, transforming temporary disruptions into opportunities for renewed (94) _________. 90
questionsEn.s: Ans: (B) manufactured

questionsEn.q: In the given passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage intently and choose the most appropriate option to fill in each blank: Postcolonial infrastructures often inhabit a schizochronic condition—a simultaneity of obsolescence and futurity. Flyovers half-finished, railway stations calcified mid-renovation, and electric grids oscillating between blackout and surplus do not signify simple malfunction. Rather, they manifest a (1) ____ temporality in which the present is neither a continuity of the past nor a stable projection of the future. These infrastructures function not as inert utilities but as affective indexes of temporal rupture. Modernity, once telegraphed through asphalt and concrete, now flickers within these arrested developments—gestures of progress suspended in bureaucratic amber. Here, functionality is beside the point. What matters is the performative (2) ____ of development: roads that signify mobility even when impassable, metros that symbolize futurity even when immobile. In this schema, infrastructure ceases to be an engineering problem and becomes a narrative technology—a spatial discourse that (3) ____ the nation-state’s promises into sedimented form. Bridges-to-be and always-rebuilding airports constitute not failure, but continuity: the continual renewal of unfinished intention. Such spatial artifacts require a recalibrated hermeneutics. To read them literally is to miss their symbolic resonance. Their disrepair is not decay but (4) ____: a visual vocabulary of state temporality, in which incompletion is the political idiom of continuity. This is the temporal grammar of anticipation without arrival. Thus, the postcolonial built environment articulates not stasis, but (5) ____—a condition where motion exists without direction, and progress is simulated through perpetual incompletion. What should come in the place of blank number (1)?
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is 'disjunctive'.

Key Points

• The passage emphasizes a fractured temporality where the present is neither a continuation of the past nor a stable projection of the future.

• The word should capture rupture, discontinuity, and simultaneity of obsolescence and futurity.

• "Disjunctive" fits perfectly as it denotes a break or lack of continuity, aligning with the schizochronic condition described.

• Other options ("stagnant", "regressive", "sovereign") do not convey the temporal rupture central to the passage.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'Option 3'.

Complete Passage:  Postcolonial infrastructures often inhabit a schizochronic condition--a simultaneity of obsolescence and futurity. Flyovers half-finished, railway stations calcified mid-renovation, and electric grids oscillating between blackout and surplus do not signify simple malfunction. Rather, they manifest a 1. disjunctive  temporality in which the present is neither a continuity of the past nor a stable projection of the future. These infrastructures function not as inert utilities but as affective indexes of temporal rupture...

Additional Information

• Stagnant: implies stillness or lack of movement, which does not capture the fractured temporality.

• Regressive: suggests backward movement, but the passage emphasizes rupture rather than reversal.

• Sovereign: relates to authority or independence, irrelevant to the temporal condition described.
