Nothing now surprised him; everything seemed natural, to be expected. S2. Sofia held out her hand, Roberto took it and bowed over it; a portière fell heavily behind him.
questionsEn.s: After S1, B logically explains Sofia’s unchanged voice and its effect on Roberto. D then generalizes Roberto’s state of mind (“Nothing now surprised him”). A supports that feeling by describing the evening as predestined/long awaited. C then narrates the parting gaze, leading naturally into S2 where they physically part with a formal gesture and the curtain falls. Learning points: (1) Cause–effect ordering: description → reaction. (2) Generalization sentences (like D) often follow a specific observation (B). (3) Narrative flow moves from internal feeling (A) to external action (C, S2). (4) Endings often contain a concrete closing image/action (S2).

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. But in college Ralph’s goals were still hazy and undefined. A. Though he continued to take classes here and there in the sciences and in the Department of Business, he also took some lower-division classes in history and philosophy and English. B. He first thought he wanted to be a doctor, or a lawyer, and he took pre-medical courses and courses in history of jurisprudence and business-law before he decided he had neither the emotional detachment necessary for medicine, nor the ability for sustained reading and memorization in the Corpus Juris Civilis, as well as the more modern texts on property and inheritance. C. But it never came. D. He continually felt he was on the brink of some momentous discovery about himself. S2. It was during this time, his lowest ebb, as he jokingly referred back to it later, that he believed he almost became an alcoholic; he was in a fraternity and he used to get drunk every night.
questionsEn.s: B explains Ralph’s initial career ideas (doctor/lawyer) and why he dropped them; A then broadens to his scattered classes, showing continued lack of direction. D fits next by stating his feeling of being close to a self-discovery, and C (“But it never came.”) logically follows as a contrast to D. This sequence leads coherently into S2 describing his lowest period. Learning points: (1) Use pronoun/reference continuity (“he,” “it”). (2) Contrast markers like “But” often follow an expectation set earlier. (3) Cause–effect and timeline help ordering. (4) Place “it never came” after the idea/hope it refers to.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. There was plenty of fish in the creek, fresh-water bream, cod, cat-fish, and tailers. A. Andy would fish for three hours at a stretch if encouraged by a ‘nibble’ or a ‘bite’ now and then - say once in twenty minutes. B. The party were fond of fish, and Andy and Dave of fishing. C. However, the creek was low, just a chain of muddy water-holes, from the hole with a few bucketfuls in it to the sizable pool with an average depth of six or seven feet, and they could get fish by bailing out the smaller holes or muddying up the water in the larger ones till the fish rose to the surface. D. The butcher was always willing to give meat in exchange for fish when they caught more than they could eat; but now it was winter, and these fish wouldn’t bite. S2. There was the cat-fish, with spikes growing out of the sides of its head, and if you got pricked you’d know it, as Dave said.
questionsEn.s: After listing fish (S1), B introduces the group and their interest in fish/fishing. A logically elaborates on Andy’s fishing behavior. D then adds a seasonal problem (winter; fish wouldn’t bite), which sets up C’s “However” explaining the creek’s low condition and alternative methods to get fish. S2 then continues with a specific description of cat-fish. Learning points: (1) General-to-specific flow improves coherence. (2) Connectives like “However” must contrast something just stated. (3) Background → action → complication → explanation is a common narrative pattern. (4) Keep related details (fishing/bites) grouped.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. I was rich and contented; I found pleasure in everything that appeals to a man of thirty-five. A. I married a year ago. B. A very beautiful, kindly and cultured young lady was my wife. C. It was a love match. D. She had been a companion to a countess not far from my estate. S2. She loved me, and her heart was full of gratitude.
questionsEn.s: A (“I married a year ago.”) naturally begins the marriage detail after S1’s life context. C (“It was a love match.”) follows as a comment on the marriage. B then describes the wife, and D adds her background, leading smoothly to S2 about her love and gratitude. Learning points: (1) Chronology often starts with the event (marriage) then evaluation then description. (2) Pronoun “She” in D needs a clear antecedent (wife) introduced in B. (3) Keep explanatory comments (love match) close to the event. (4) End should support S2’s emotional conclusion.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. It was long after midnight when we locked up the Englishman and went to bed ourselves. A. Noble took it very quietly. B. I having thought of the same thing myself (among many others) said no, because it was more than likely the English wouldn't shoot our men, and anyhow it wasn't to be supposed the Brigade who were always up and down with the second battalion and knew the Englishman well would be likely to want them bumped off. C. As I blew out the candle I told Noble what Jeremiah Donovan had told me. D. After we had been in bed about an hour he asked me did I think we ought to tell the Englishmen. S2. "I think so," says Noble.
questionsEn.s: The logical flow is: after locking up and going to bed (S1), the narrator tells Noble what he heard while blowing out the candle (C). Noble reacts quietly (A). Later, Noble asks whether they should tell the Englishmen (D), and the narrator answers “no” with reasons (B). Finally, Noble concludes, “I think so,” (S2). Learning points: (1) Time markers help: “As I blew out the candle” precedes “After we had been in bed about an hour”. (2) Pronoun reference: “he asked me” needs a prior setup of conversation. (3) Reaction sentence (A) follows the information (C). (4) Long reasoning (B) answers a question (D). (5) Direct speech often closes the paragraph.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Then the spring came, and all over the country there were little blossoms and little birds. A. The only people who were pleased were the Snow and the Frost. B. Only in the garden of the Selfish Giant it was still winter. C. The birds did not care to sing in it as there were no children, and the trees forgot to blossom. D. Once a beautiful flower put its head out from the grass, but when it saw the notice-board it was so sorry for the children that it slipped back into the ground again and went off to sleep. S2. "Spring has forgotten this garden," they cried, "so we will live here all the year round."
questionsEn.s: After spring arrives everywhere (S1), contrast is introduced: only the Selfish Giant’s garden remains winter (B). Then the effects in the garden are described: birds don’t sing and trees don’t blossom (C). A specific incident follows: a flower appears but retreats on seeing the notice-board (D). Finally, Snow and Frost are pleased and decide to stay (A), leading into their concluding remark in S2. Learning points: (1) Contrast connector: “Only...” naturally follows the general statement about spring. (2) General conditions (C) precede a specific example (D). (3) Snow and Frost being pleased (A) logically comes after winter persists. (4) S2 is direct speech of Snow/Frost, so A should lead into it. (5) Coherence often uses: general → contrast → details → example → conclusion.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. So why develop your financial genius? A. I can tell you why I have been developing this area of my intelligence. B. Not because I need to, but because I want to. C. Only you can answer that. D. I do it because I want to make money fast. S2. It is a fascinating learning process.
questionsEn.s: After S1 (a question), “Only you can answer that” (C) logically responds. Then A introduces the speaker’s explanation (“I can tell you why…”), followed by D giving a reason (money fast), and B refining/qualifying the motive (“Not because… but because…”), ending with S2 as a concluding remark. Other sequences break the question–answer flow or place explanations before the response. Learning points: look for direct replies to questions; identify pronoun reference (“that”); keep cause→clarification order; end with a summarizing sentence.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Sofia stood listening to the noise of the departing carriage which bore away her mother and sister. A. As a child, when some wrong or injustice had been done her, she had cried all alone, in the dark, and the habit had remained with her. B. She was left alone, quite alone, as she had always wished to be left. C. Certainly in these moments of complete solitude the consciousness of a great grief came over her; D. Now, alone in the great drawing room, beneath the brightly lighted chandelier, her hands inert, her head resting against the back of her chair, her face wore an expression of great sorrow, the vivid reflection of a serious inward conflict. S2. the sentiment of the reality, long repulsed, became clear, distinct, and cruel.
questionsEn.s: After S1, B naturally follows (she is now alone). Then A provides background about her childhood habit of crying alone, supporting the solitude theme. D gives a detailed present scene description (“Now, alone…”), and C transitions into her internal realization of grief, leading into S2’s conclusion. Other orders disrupt the narrative time flow (present scene vs past habit) or weaken the linkage to S2. Learning points: track time markers (“Now,” “As a child”); keep background before detailed present description or as logical support; ensure emotional crescendo to the concluding sentence.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. The next morning I went to see her, but when I entered the hut, she, poor thing, was already stark and cold. A. They were good folk. B. The babies were left alone. C. In dying, she had rolled on to this child and crushed her leg. D. The village folk came to the hut, washed the body, laid her out, made a coffin, and buried her. S2. What was to be done with them?
questionsEn.s: After S1 reveals the woman is dead, the immediate detail explaining the tragedy is C (she rolled onto the child and crushed her leg). Next, D logically follows as community actions after death (washing, laying out, coffin, burial). Then A provides a general remark about the villagers (“They were good folk”), and B sets up the concluding concern about the children being alone, which leads naturally to S2 (“What was to be done with them?”). Learning points: (1) Look for cause → aftermath → evaluation → problem. (2) Pronoun reference (“them” in S2) must be introduced (babies). (3) Events after death usually precede general commentary. (4) Coherence depends on time order and referents.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. One day in autumn on my way back from a remote part of the country I caught cold and fell ill. A. He prescribed me the usual sudorific, ordered a mustard plaster to be put on, very deftly slid a five-rouble note up his sleeve, coughing drily and looking away as he did so, and then was getting up to go home, but somehow fell into talk and remained. B. I was exhausted with feverishness; I foresaw a sleepless night and was glad of a little chat with a pleasant companion. C. Fortunately, the fever attacked me in the district town at the inn; I sent for the doctor. D. In half an hour the district doctor appeared, a thin, dark-haired man of middle height. S2. Tea was served.
questionsEn.s: From S1 (fell ill), the next logical step is C (he was in an inn in a district town and sent for the doctor). Then D (doctor arrived). Then A (doctor examined/prescribed and the episode with the note; then he stayed to talk). Then B (narrator’s state and relief at conversation), leading naturally to S2 (tea served). Learning points: (1) Trigger event → action taken → arrival → detailed interaction → reflection. (2) Time marker “In half an hour” must follow “sent for the doctor.” (3) Detailed prescription scene must follow doctor’s arrival. (4) Ending with tea fits after companionship is established.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. There was another guest who interested me. A. He was a personage. B. At first glance one could tell he was an honoured guest and stood in the same relation to the host as the host to the gentleman of the whiskers. C. But he was of quite a different order. D. They called him Julian Mastakovich. S2. The host and hostess said no end of amiable things to him, were most attentive, wining him, hovering over him, bringing guests up to be introduced, but never leading him to anyone else,
questionsEn.s: After S1 introduces “another guest,” C contrasts him with someone previously mentioned (“a different order”), then A characterizes him (“a personage”), then D gives his name, and B adds how his honoured status was evident at first glance—leading into S2 describing the special attention he received. Learning points: (1) Contrast marker “But” (C) usually comes early after introduction. (2) Naming (D) often follows initial description. (3) Status explanation (B) supports why hosts were attentive in S2. (4) Maintain pronoun clarity: “He” must consistently refer to the same guest.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. For the first time it occurred to me that if things worked out the way everyone was hoping, I'd be going halfway around the world to live with a man I hadn't even met. A. It would be ungrateful. B. Don't send me so far away, I wanted to cry, but of course I didn't. C. Would I ever see my parents again? D. Father had worked so hard to find this match for me. S2. Besides, wasn't it every woman's destiny, as Mother was always telling me, to leave the known for the unknown?
questionsEn.s: The best sequence is CBAD. After S1, the speaker’s immediate worry is about parents (C). Then comes an emotional reaction (B). Next, the speaker checks herself by noting it would be ungrateful (A), and finally gives the reason—father worked hard to find the match (D)—before concluding with S2 about destiny. Learning points: (1) Look for question-to-emotion flow (C → B). (2) “It would be ungrateful” (A) needs a prior impulse to complain (B). (3) “Father had worked…” (D) explains why complaining would be ungrateful. (4) S2 generalises the idea into “destiny,” so it naturally closes. (5) Pronouns and tone shifts help identify coherence.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. I was an outsider, and, as I had no special matters to air, I was able to spend the evening independently of the others. A. He was tall, rather thin, very serious, and well dressed. B. He was the first to attract my attention. C. There was another gentleman present who like myself had just stumbled upon this affair of domestic bliss. D. His appearance was not that of a man of birth or high family. S2. Apparently he had no heart for the family festivities.
questionsEn.s: The best sequence is CBDA. After S1, the narrator notes another outsider-like gentleman (C). Then she says he attracted her attention (B). Next she describes his looks (D then A): first a general social impression (not of high birth) (D), then physical description (A). S2 concludes that he had no interest in the festivities. Learning points: (1) Introduce the person before describing (C → B). (2) “He” needs an antecedent—provided by (C). (3) General assessment (D) often precedes detailed description (A). (4) S2 summarises attitude, so it closes well. (5) Maintain narrator perspective and logical progression.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence. S1. Sofia did not raise her eyes from her work, and her slim fingers fairly flew over the delicate lace. A. She hummed a few bars of a song and recited a verse, but Sofia appeared not to hear. B. But Lulu wandered about the room, moving the ornaments on the shelves or opening a drawer to gaze absently into it. C. Then Lulu, who was not blessed with too much patience, decided to put the question boldly, and, planting herself in front of her sister, she asked: D. It was clear that she wished either to do or to say something but was abashed by her elder sister's grave manner. S2. "Sofia, do you know what Mademoiselle Jeannette told me?"
questionsEn.s: After S1, D logically explains Sofia’s grave manner affecting Lulu. B begins with “But Lulu…” introducing Lulu’s restlessness against Sofia’s focused work. A follows as Lulu tries humming/reciting to get attention. C then shows Lulu finally asking directly, leading into S2 (the question). Learning points: (1) Track contrast markers like “But”; (2) Pronoun/reference continuity (she/her/sister); (3) Look for action escalation: wandering → trying to attract → asking; (4) S2 must follow the “she asked:” cue; (5) Choose the option that places the dialogue trigger immediately before S2.

test.instructions: Standard CBT Pattern Exam. Positive Marks: +1, Negative Marks: -0.25. Total Questions: 25.

test.title: Set - 9

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence. S1. He remained a day in order to learn the art, because he thought he might be able to turn it to use later on, if by chance he should fail to find other work in Batavia. A. Neither on the first nor the second day had he realized how lonely he was, because he was captivated by the grand idea of earning enough money to buy two buffaloes, whereas his father had never had more than one, and was too excited over the prospect of seeing Adinda again to grieve over his departure. B. The following day toward evening he thanked his host and departed. C. He had left in an anxious hope. D. As soon as it was dark, and no one could see him, he took out the Melati leaves Adinda had given him, for he was sad, thinking that he would not see her for so long. S2. The prospect of seeing her again so occupied his heart that on leaving Badoer and passing the tree, he felt something akin to joy, as if the thirty-six moons were already past.
questionsEn.s: After S1 (he stayed a day to learn), B naturally gives the departure event next. D then describes what he did at night after departure (Melati leaves; sadness). A reflects on his emotional state across the first/second day and his excitement about seeing Adinda again. C (“He had left in an anxious hope.”) sums up his departure mindset, leading smoothly into S2 about joy at the prospect of meeting her again. Learning points: (1) Time markers: “The following day…” must precede later-night details; (2) Cause-effect linking (departure → night reflection); (3) Emotional arc consistency; (4) Place concluding general sentence near the end; (5) Ensure S2 connects to the final emotional state.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are named A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. She wished she had an hour to visit her old flat in 164th Street - just a turn around the block would be enough, but there wasn't time. A. "The Prince of Love," she said to herself. B. An old resentment rose against Honora, who was a born spoilsport and would spoil this trip for her if she could. C. She walked on, getting her directions, brooding a little because she had been such a city girl once, thinking only of dress and a good time, and now she hardly knew one street from another. D. She went into the first moving picture theatre she saw because she liked the name of it. S2. It was about two beautiful young things, a boy with black wavy hair and a girl with curly golden hair, who loved each other and had great troubles, but it all came well in the end, and all the time it was just one fine ballroom or garden after another, and such beautiful clothes!
questionsEn.s: The sequence BCDA is coherent: after S1, she feels resentment (B) about Honora spoiling the trip; then she continues walking and brooding while taking directions (C); then she enters a moving picture theatre (D); then she reacts to the theatre name with the quote (A), leading naturally into S2 describing what the film was about. Learning points: (1) place emotional reaction sentences (resentment) near the trigger; (2) action progression: walking → entering theatre; (3) quoted line (A) best fits after seeing the theatre name; (4) S2 clearly refers to the movie, so D must precede S2; (5) use “because” clauses (C) as narrative continuation.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are named A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. I knew it was the most famous spot in Honolulu and I entered it with a lively curiosity. A. It is a large square room, with three entrances, and opposite the bar, which runs the length of it, two corners have been partitioned off into little cubicles. B. There is a portrait of him, in oils, in a rich gold frame; but there are also two prints of Queen Victoria. C. Legend states that they were built so that King Kalakaua might drink there without being seen by his subjects, and it is pleasant to think that in one or other of these he may have sat over his bottle, a coal-black potentate, with Robert Louis Stevenson. D. You get to it by a narrow passage from King Street, and in the passage are offices, so that thirsty souls may be supposed bound for one of these just as well as for the saloon. S2. On the walls, besides, are old line engravings of the eighteenth century, one of which, and heaven knows how it got there, is after a theatrical picture by de Wilde; and there are oleographs from the Christmas supplements of the Graphic and the Illustrated London News of twenty years ago.
questionsEn.s: DACB fits: after entering (S1), the narrator explains how you get to it via a narrow passage (D), then describes the room layout (A). Next, “two corners partitioned into cubicles” leads to the legend about why those cubicles existed (C). Finally, details of wall items/portraits (B) smoothly connect to S2 which continues describing engravings and oleographs on the walls. Learning points: (1) route/entry description usually comes before interior description; (2) pronoun reference “they” in C refers to “cubicles” in A; (3) descriptive inventory (B) aligns with S2’s wall-description continuation; (4) check cohesion via referents and logical flow; (5) legends/explanations often follow the object being described.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are named A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. The church was empty and dark. A. In perfect silence, and with his back turned towards me, he was running over the organ keys with one hand while managing the stops with the other. B. Far away there gleamed a feeble light, like a faint star in the sky; it was the lamp burning on the high altar. C. And the organ sounded, but in an indescribable manner. D. By its flickering light, which only helped to make the deep horror of the shadows the more intense, I saw—I saw—Mother, do not disbelieve it— a man. S2. It seemed as if each note were a sob somewhere in the metal tube, which vibrated under the pressure of the air compressed within it and gave forth a low, almost imperceptible tone, yet exact and true.
questionsEn.s: BDAC is logical: after S1, the distant altar lamp is noticed (B). That lamp’s flickering light then enables the narrator to see a man (D). Next comes the detailed action of the man at the organ in silence (A), followed by the statement that the organ sounded in an indescribable manner (C), which leads naturally into S2 describing the quality of each note. Learning points: (1) “By its flickering light” in D refers to the lamp in B; (2) A describes the man’s action, so it should follow D (which introduces him); (3) C is a bridge to S2’s sound-description; (4) maintain sensory sequence: sight → discovery → action → sound; (5) match cause-effect cues (“By its… I saw…”).

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Tears gushed from his eyes; he drove on at random. A. The night was tolerably clear. B. Vladimir drove towards it. C. He saw, not far off, a little village, consisting of four or five houses. D. Meanwhile the storm had subsided, the clouds dispersed, and before him lay a level plain covered with a white, undulating carpet. S2. At the first cottage he jumped out of the sledge, ran to the window and began to knock.
questionsEn.s: The logical flow is: after driving randomly (S1), the scene description should set the weather/visibility and terrain (D), then mention the clear night (A), then he spots the village (C), then he drives toward it (B), leading naturally to reaching the first cottage (S2). Hence sequence DACB. Learning points: place setting before action; introduce object (village) before “towards it”; maintain cause-effect; watch pronoun/reference (“it” must have an antecedent).

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Two days and two nights did Peter sleep without once awakening. A. He looked; there were two bags of gold. B. When he came to himself, on the third day, he looked long at all the corners of his hut but in vain did he endeavour to recollect what had taken place; his memory was like a miser's pocket from which you cannot entice a quarter of a kopek. C. Stretching himself, he heard something clash at his feet. D. Then, only as if in a dream, he recollected that he had been seeking for treasure and that something had frightened him in the woods. S2. But at what price he had obtained it, and how, he could by no means tell.
questionsEn.s: After S1 (he slept), B logically follows (he came to himself on the third day, memory unclear). Then C (he hears something clash at his feet), then A (he sees two bags of gold), then D (he recollects the treasure-seeking in a dreamlike way), leading into S2 (he cannot tell at what price/how he obtained it). Hence BCAD. Learning points: time markers (“on the third day”) should appear early; sensory trigger (clash) precedes discovery (gold); recollection comes after discovery; ensure narrative coherence.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Confidence is either a gift or an acquisition. A. Whenever an opportunity is accepted, opposite effects follow: the fact of acceptance tends to strengthen fain in self, even though the outcome be not altogether satisfactory, provided the will persists to accept other opportunities. B. Whenever an opportunity is declined because of fear, confidence is weakened; that the lack of it is emphasized in consciousness. C. Either vibrations are induced which injuriously affect the subconscious mind or confirm existing psychic states. D. In the latter case, it is born of opportunities successfully taken. S2. Under this method the growth of confidence is not stopped by occasional failures.
questionsEn.s: The correct sequence is **D → B → C → A**. After S1 introduces confidence as gift/acquisition, **D** logically explains the “acquisition” route (“In the latter case…”). Then **B** contrasts what happens when opportunities are declined (fear weakens confidence). **C** follows B by explaining the psychological effect (“Either vibrations are induced…”), and **A** completes the contrast by describing the positive effect when opportunities are accepted, which leads smoothly into S2’s conclusion about growth despite occasional failures. Learning points: (1) look for linkers like “in the latter case,” (2) maintain contrast pairs: declined vs accepted, (3) ensure pronoun/connector references are resolved, (4) place general-to-specific and cause-to-effect logically.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. After the repast, play is proposed. A. A dispute arises on some circumstances in the game, and the disputants grow warm one of his intimate friends throws a dice box at his head and strikes out one of his eyes. B. A little play with one's intimate friends is a harmless pastime. C. The philosopher Mennon is carried home to his house, dark and penniless, with the loss of an eye. D. He plays and loses all that is in his purse, and four times as much on his word. S2. He sleeps out his debauch, and when his head has got a little clear, he sends his servant to the Receiver General of the finances of Nineveh to draw a little money to pay his debts of honour to his intimate friends.
questionsEn.s: **B → D → A → C** fits best. After S1 (play is proposed), **B** gives a general comment about playing with friends. **D** then narrates what happens: he plays and loses money. **A** escalates the events into a dispute and injury. **C** logically follows as the consequence: he is carried home injured, dark and penniless. This sets up S2, where he later clears his head and arranges money to pay debts. Learning points: (1) arrange events chronologically, (2) place general statement before specific incident, (3) ensure cause (dispute/injury) precedes result (carried home), (4) watch for coherence with S2’s “debts of honour.”

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Having thus laid his little plan of philosophy in his closet, Menon put his head out of the window. A. The one was old, and appeared quite at her ease. B. The other was young, handsome, and seemingly much agitated: she sighed, she wept, and seemed on that account still more beautiful. C. Our philosopher was touched, not, to be sure, with the beauty of the lady (he was too much determined not to feel any uneasiness of that kind) but with the distress which he saw her in. D. He saw two women walking under the plane trees near his house. S2. He came downstairs and accosted the young Ninevite in the design of consoling her with philosophy.
questionsEn.s: After S1 (he looks out of the window), it logically follows that he **sees two women** (D). Then the description naturally splits into “the one” (old) (A) and “the other” (young and agitated) (B). After observing their state, the philosopher is moved by her distress (C), which leads coherently to S2 where he comes downstairs to console the young woman. Learning points: pronoun/connector cues (“the one…the other”) fix A and B order; observation precedes reaction; maintain character continuity (young Ninevite in S2 aligns with “the other” in B).

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. What a night! A. Alas, how shall we paint the emotions that arose in her soul, that divided, tore it between love and virtue? B. What a dreadful night for Lydia! C. They led her to the altar as it were to punishment. D. She adored Lausua, she detested Mezentius, she was sacrificing herself to her father's interests, delivering herself up to the object of her hatred, tearing herself forever from an adored lover. S2. Barbarous Mezentius! Thou art content to reign over the heart by violence and fear!
questionsEn.s: S1 sets an exclamatory tone. Next, specifying whose night it was (“for Lydia”) (B) is natural. Then the text explores her inner conflict/emotions (A), followed by the detailed explanation of her situation (D). Finally, the narrative moves to the action of being led to the altar (C), which connects to the condemnation of Mezentius in S2. Learning points: general → specific flow; emotion framing often precedes detailed circumstances; action (“led her to the altar”) fits after explaining why it feels like punishment.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. I do not believe that chickens await the hour when the housewife brings their corn with as much anxiety as Peter awaited the evening. A. How long it was! B. But now the sun has set. C. Evidently God's day had lost its end somewhere. D. He kept looking to see whether the shadows of the trees were not lengthening, whether the sun was not turning red towards setting; and, the longer he watched, the more impatient he grew. S2. The sky is red only on one side, and it is already growing dark.
questionsEn.s: After S1 (Peter anxiously awaited evening), the next logical sentence is his repeated watching of the setting signs (D). Then his impatience is summarized (“How long it was!”) (A). Next, the narrator comments on the unusual delay (“God's day had lost its end…”) (C). Then the transition “But now the sun has set” (B) leads smoothly into S2 describing the sky and darkness. Learning points: keep cause → reaction order; “But now” signals a late-stage transition, so B must come near the end; descriptive continuity with sunset/dark in S2 supports B right before S2.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence, keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.' A. Christ, the special manifestation of the Absolute is known and knowable. B. The Word has two manifestations—the general one of Nature and the special one of the great Incarnations of God: Krishna, Buddha, Jesus and Ramakrishna. C. The Hindu calls this maya, the manifestation of God, because it is the power of God. D. The Absolute reflecting through the universe is what we call Nature. S2. The Absolute cannot be known; We cannot know the Father, only the Son.
questionsEn.s: The coherent flow is: after S1 introduces “the Word,” C introduces the Hindu concept of maya as God’s manifestation, D defines Nature as the Absolute reflected through the universe, B then explains the two manifestations (general Nature and special incarnations), and A narrows to Christ as the special manifestation that is knowable, leading naturally into S2 (“only the Son”). Hence the correct sequence is C–D–B–A. Learning points: (1) Use definitional links (Nature ↔ Absolute) to order; (2) move from general concept to specific example; (3) pronoun/reference tracking (“this” in C needs an antecedent idea of manifestation); (4) concluding sentence S2 aligns with “Son/Christ” just before it; (5) keep thematic progression (Word → manifestation → Nature/incarnations → Christ).

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. At last Vladimir perceived that he was going in the wrong direction. A. His horse could scarcely move forward. B. He turned to the right now. C. He had now been on the road for more than an hour. D. He stopped, began to think, to recollect, and compare, and he felt convinced that he ought to have turned to the right. S2. Jadrino could not be far off.
questionsEn.s: After S1 (realising he is wrong), D logically follows: he stops and thinks and becomes convinced he should have turned right; then B shows the corrective action (he turns right). The remaining details can then follow to sustain narration: A (horse could scarcely move forward) adds difficulty in progress, and C gives the time reference (“more than an hour”), culminating in S2 (destination not far). Thus the best sequence among the options is D–B–A–C. Learning points: (1) Cause → reflection → action is a common narrative order; (2) D contains the decision, so it must precede B (action); (3) descriptive details (horse/time) often come after the turning point; (4) S2 is a concluding inference, so it stays last; (5) in ordering, look for “now” indicating immediate next action.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. I'm doing fine, except I've got no appetite. A. I keep hearing: "Goodness, you look awful!" B. The atmosphere is stifling, sluggish, leaden. C. My nerves often get the better of me, especially on Sundays; that is when I really feel miserable. D. I must admit they're doing their best to keep me in condition: they're plying me with dextrose, cod-liver oil, brewer's yeast and calcium. S2. Outside, you don't hear a single bird, and a deathly, oppressive silence hangs over the house and clings to me as if it were going to drag me into the deepest regions of the underworld.
questionsEn.s: The logical flow is S1 → A → D → C → B → S2. After S1 (no appetite), A introduces what others say (“you look awful!”), D explains the care being given (dextrose, cod-liver oil, etc.), C describes the speaker’s nerves and Sunday misery, and B sets the heavy atmospheric tone leading into S2’s deathly silence outside. Learning points: (1) Look for cause–effect and topic flow. (2) Pronoun/reference links guide order. (3) Mood-building sentences usually come just before atmospheric closing. (4) Eliminate options that break coherence between A, D, C, B.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. In front of this building, overlooking the river, is a garden, where the once well-trimmed box borders that used to define the walks now grow wild as they list. A. The rich vegetation of those weeds that we call foul adorns the sloping shore. B. The wall fruit grows like hedges against the walls. C. Several willows that spring from the Loire have grown as rapidly as the hedge that encloses it and half conceal the house. D. Fruit trees, neglected for the last ten years, no longer yield their harvest, and their shoots form coppices. S2. Paths once gravelled are overgrown with moss, but to tell the truth, there is no trace of a path.
questionsEn.s: The logical sequence is S1 → C → A → D → B → S2. After S1 (wild garden by river), C introduces willows from the Loire half-concealing the house, A describes the rich weed vegetation on the sloping shore, D notes neglected fruit trees forming coppices, and B adds wall fruit growing like hedges, before S2 closes with overgrown paths. Learning points: (1) Use geography (river → shore → trees → walls) to track flow. (2) Specific images often follow general scene. (3) Look for natural progression of description. (4) Eliminate options that disturb visual logic.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. When the short days of winter came, dusk fell before we had well eaten our dinners. A. Our shouts echoed in the silent street. B. When we met in the street the houses had grown sombre. C. The space of sky above us was the colour of ever-changing violet and towards it the lamps of the street lifted their feeble lanterns. D. The cold air stung us and we played till our bodies glowed. S2. The career of our play brought us through dark muddy lanes behind the houses, where we ran the gauntlet of the rough tribes from the cottages, to the back doors of the dark dripping gardens where odours arose from the ashpits, to the dark odorous stables where a coachman smoothed and combed the horse or shook music from the buckled harness.
questionsEn.s: After S1 sets the winter-evening scene, B logically follows (meeting in the street; houses look sombre). Then C describes the sky and street lamps, expanding the dusk imagery. D fits next as it describes playing in the cold air. A (“Our shouts echoed…”) naturally follows the playing/action before S2’s extended description of where their play took them. Learning points: (1) Identify scene-setting (S1) and concluding movement (S2). (2) Use connectors like time/setting → description → action → sound/result. (3) Look for pronoun/idea continuity (“we met,” “we played,” “our shouts”). (4) In para-jumbles, sensory description often precedes action-based sentences.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. There, for the first time, had the painter caught sight of Laurella who, with her pitcher on her head, had passed by without taking any notice of him. A. A very ungentle ball came knocking against his shins as a reminder that this was not the spot to choose for meditation. B. But the young boatman who had thrown the ball stood silent among his friends, in such an attitude of defiance that the stranger had found it more advisable to go his way and avoid discussion. C. The Neapolitan, struck by her appearance, stood still and gazed after her, not heeding that he was standing in the very midst of the game, which, with two steps, he might have cleared. D. He looked round, as if in expectation of some excuse. S2. Still, this little encounter had been spoken of, particularly at the time when the painter had been pressing his suit to Laurella.
questionsEn.s: After S1 introduces Laurella and the painter noticing her, C naturally follows by explaining his reaction (he stands still, gazing). Then A occurs as a consequence (a ball hits his shins because he is in the middle of the game). D follows as his immediate response (he looks around, expecting an excuse). Finally B completes the encounter by describing the boatman’s defiant stance and why the stranger leaves, leading smoothly to S2 referencing how the encounter was later discussed. Learning points: (1) Cause-effect ordering is crucial (gazing → gets hit by ball). (2) “He looked round” must follow an incident prompting it. (3) “But” in B signals contrast and fits after the situation is established. (4) Match character references consistently (painter/Neapolitan/stranger).

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Down in the dust though my spirit was, I might have tried to strike him for those words if at that moment I had not noticed something very surprising. A. When, therefore, Mr. Preston gave me the coat which he had picked up from the floor, I saw with terror that my own was already hanging on my arm and that the two were alike in every way. B. My coat had cost more money than most men could spend, and it had been made especially for me. C. I remembered that the strange being who had so mysteriously entered and left the room had had a coat. D. It was different, I thought, from every other coat in the world. S2. No one else in the group had been wearing one.
questionsEn.s: The correct sequence is BDAC. First, B introduces the coat’s cost/special making; D follows naturally stating it was unique; A then presents the surprise of two identical coats (his own already on his arm); C then recalls the mysterious being had a coat, setting up S2 that no one else wore one. Learning points: (1) Look for pronoun/reference links (“it,” “the coat”). (2) “Therefore” in A indicates it follows earlier context about the coat. (3) Unique → shock at identical is a logical progression. (4) End sentence S2 must be supported by the recall in C.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. You can testify that I was never a coward. A. All my life long, in Jaen, in Madrid, and elsewhere, I have walked the streets at all hours, alone and unarmed, and if I have chanced to run upon suspicious-looking persons, thieves, or mere sneaking beggars, they have had to get out of my way or take to their heels. B. I fought a dupl once, when I had to, like any other man. C. But if the person turned out to be a solitary woman, standing still or walking, and I was also alone, with no one in sight in any direction, then (laugh) if you want to, but believe me) I would be all covered over with goose-flesh; vague fears would assail me; I would think about beings of the other world, about imaginary existences, and about all the superstitious stories which would make me laugh under other circumstances. D. Just after I had left the School of Engineers, my workmen in Despeafierros revolted, and I fought them with stick and pistol until I made them submit. S2. I would quicken my pace, or else turn back, and would not get over my fright in the least until safe in my own house.
questionsEn.s: The correct order is BDAC. B provides a general brave act (a duel); D adds another strong example (fighting revolting workmen), supporting S1. A then broadens the claim with habitual fearlessness in streets. C introduces the contrast (“But…”) revealing his irrational fear when encountering a solitary woman, which leads logically to S2 about quickening pace/turning back until safe. Learning points: (1) “But” in C signals a turning point after examples of bravery. (2) Arrange from general claim → supporting examples → contrast. (3) Time marker “Just after…” in D fits early-life evidence. (4) S2 must follow the “fear” situation in C.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered as S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. An enormous lion advances. A. Terror and pity seize on every breast. B. In a short time, the sound of clarions animates him; he replies by his roarings; his shaggy mane is erected around his monstrous head; he lashes his loins with his tail, and the fire begins to issue from his sparkling eyeballs. C. At first, with a calm pride, he traverses the arena, throwing his dreadful looks round the amphitheatre that environs him; a confused murmur announces the terror that he inspires. D. The affrighted populace wish and dread to see the wretch appear who is to be delivered up to the rage of this monster. S2. The combatant, whom Mezentius' guards themselves had taken for Phanor, presents himself.
questionsEn.s: The sequence CBDA is coherent. C describes the lion’s initial movement in the arena; B then intensifies the description as sounds excite him; D shifts to the crowd’s anticipation of the victim/combatant; A captures the crowd’s emotions (terror and pity) before S2 introduces the combatant who finally appears. Learning points: (1) “At first” in C indicates an early position. (2) B continues physical description logically after C. (3) Crowd-focused sentences (D, A) should precede the arrival in S2. (4) Maintain narrative flow: lion → escalation → crowd reaction → entry of combatant.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence. S1. He was older than I. A. But his strange, heavy, almost waxen face was not lined by experience. B. And sometimes that face, in stillness when he listened to me playing, with the heavy eyelids folded over eyes that always disturbed me by their absolute absence of light, seemed to me like a mask, as if his real face, the face that truly reflected all the life he had led in the world before he met me, before, even, I was born, as though that face lay underneath this mask. C. Rather, experience seemed to have washed it perfectly smooth, like a stone on a beach whose fissures have been eroded by successive tides. D. He was much older than I; there were streaks of pure silver in his dark mane. S2. Or else, elsewhere.
questionsEn.s:
The correct sequence is DACB.
- S1 establishes that the subject is older than the narrator.
- D reinforces and expands on this age difference with concrete physical evidence ("streaks of pure silver in his dark mane").
- A introduces a contrast using "But," noting that despite his age, his face was surprisingly unlined by experience.
- C follows naturally from A with "Rather," providing the explanation for why his face appeared unlined—it had been smoothed by experience like a stone eroded by tides.
- B develops the description further, exploring the mask-like quality of this smooth, expressionless face.
- S2 concludes with an enigmatic suggestion that his true self exists somewhere hidden or elsewhere.
This sequence creates a smooth progression from general observation of age → physical evidence → description of face → explanation of appearance → deeper reflection on hidden nature.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence. S1. It was a blazing hot day in August. A. For myself, my term of service in India had trained me to stand heat better than cold, and a thermometer at ninety was no hardship. B. Our blinds were half drawn, and Holmes lay curled upon the sofa, reading and re-reading a letter which he had received by the morning post. C. Baker Street was like an oven, and the glare of the sunlight upon the yellow brickwork of the house across the road was painful to the eye. D. It was hard to believe that these were the same walls which loomed so gloomily through the fogs of winter. S2. But the morning paper was uninteresting.
questionsEn.s:
The sequence CDBA follows a logical narrative flow.
- S1 establishes the setting: a blazing hot August day.
- C expands on the heat's impact on Baker Street specifically, describing it as "like an oven" with painful glare on the brickwork—moving from general weather to specific location.
- D provides a contrasting reflection, comparing the current bright, harsh scene with the gloomy winter appearance of the same walls.
- B shifts focus from outside to inside, describing the indoor scene with Holmes on the sofa and half-drawn blinds (a response to the heat).
- A presents the narrator's personal perspective on the heat, explaining his tolerance for it due to his Indian service.
- S2 transitions to a new topic (the morning paper), connected by "But" to shift from the heat discussion.
This creates a camera-like movement: weather → street outside → contrast with winter → inside the room → narrator's reaction → shift to new topic.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence. S1. Jovinian, however, having quitted the water, sought in every possible direction for his horse and clothes and, to his utter astonishment, could find neither. A. "Miserable man that I am," said he, "to what a strait am I reduced! B. I will then ride on to the palace and strictly investigate the cause of this extraordinary conduct. C. There is, I remember, a knight who lives close by; I will go to him and command his attendance and service. D. Vexed beyond measure at the circumstance (for he was completely naked and saw no one near to assist him), he began to reflect upon what course he should pursue. S2. Some shall smart for it."
questionsEn.s:
The correct sequence is DACB, which follows a clear emotional and logical progression.
- S1 introduces the situation: Jovinian has come out of the water and cannot find his horse or clothes.
- D comes next because it explains his immediate condition and reaction: he is completely naked, helpless, and begins to think about what he should do.
- A naturally follows D as his first emotional response after reflecting on his miserable condition. He cries out, “Miserable man that I am...”
- C then gives the practical solution he thinks of: he remembers a nearby knight and decides to go to him for assistance and service.
- B follows C because after getting help from the knight, he plans to ride to the palace and investigate the strange conduct.
- S2 completes the thought with his angry threat: “Some shall smart for it.”
Thus, the logical order is: S1 → D → A → C → B → S2.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. From beyond the sea came hosts of Greeks, armed for war and bent upon the conquest of the city. A. The cry was for vengeance, and heroes and warriors from every city and town joined hands and vowed vengeance upon Troy. B. He had stolen and carried away from her shores the most beautiful of all her women, even Helen, the wife of Menelaus of Sparta. C. They came in a thousand little ships, with sails and oars, and landed on the beach at the foot of the plain. D. They came because one of the princes of Troy, Paris by name, had done a grievous wrong to Greece. S2. They built huts and tents along the shore; they kindled fires; they threw up a breastwork of earth and stones around their camp; they defied the warriors of Troy to come out on the plain and meet them in battle.
questionsEn.s:
The logical flow is: reason first (D: why they came), then the specific wrong (B: Helen’s abduction), then the wider response (A: Greeks vow vengeance), then the arrival details (C: ships and landing), leading into S2 (camp built). Hence DBAC.
Learning points: (1) Coherence often follows: cause → detail → reaction → action. (2) Pronoun tracking: “He” in B refers back to Paris introduced in D. (3) Broad-to-specific sequencing helps. (4) S2 continues naturally after landing (C). (5) Look for dependency links (Paris → He).

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. As for Simmons, he, it was held, was fortunate in that capable wife. A. Nobody could tell what might not have happened to Tommy Simmons if there had been no Mrs. Simmons to take care of him. B. He had no vices (even his pipe departed him after his marriage), and Mrs. Simmons had ingrained on him divers exotic virtues. C. He was a moderately good carpenter and joiner, but no man of the world, and he wanted to be one. D. He was a meek and quiet man, with a boyish face and sparse, limp whiskers. S2. He went solemnly to chapel every Sunday, under a tall hat, and put a penny - one returned to him for the purpose out of his week's wages - in the plate.
questionsEn.s:
After S1 (fortunate because of his wife), it makes sense to describe Simmons (C: his limited worldliness), then his appearance/temperament (A? actually D fits better before A), then D (meek, quiet, boyish face), then A (what might have happened without Mrs. Simmons), and then B (no vices; wife ingrained virtues), leading to S2 (chapel routine). The option matching the intended coherence is CADB.
Learning points: (1) Build from general claim to supporting details. (2) Character description (C, D) usually precedes consequences (A). (3) Wife’s influence is reinforced in A and B. (4) S2 is an example of his virtuous routine. (5) Look for narrative escalation: trait → dependence → reform.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. It was a close, musty, ill-ventilated place, as might be expected, since its inmate seldom left it. A. A thick dark veil covered her face, but it was cut off close at her upper lip and disclosed a perfectly shaped mouth and a delicately rounded chin. B. From keeping beasts in a cage, the woman seemed, by some retribution of fate, to have become herself a beast in a cage. C. She sat now in a broken armchair in the shadowy corner of the room. D. Long years of inaction had coarsened the lines of her figure, but at some period it must have been beautiful, and was still full and voluptuous. S2. I could well conceive that she had indeed been a very remarkable woman.
questionsEn.s:
The best sequence is BCDA: after describing the place (S1), the text logically introduces the woman’s caged condition (B), then her position in the room (C), then her veiled face details (A), followed by her figure description (D), and concludes with the overall impression (S2).

Why other options are wrong: Other orders break the flow from general description → position → facial details → figure details → concluding remark.

Learning points: (1) Move from general setting to the subject. (2) Keep physical positioning before close-up description. (3) Maintain descriptive coherence (face/figure). (4) Ensure smooth link to the concluding sentence. (5) Look for logical zoom-in: room → person → details.

The best order is DACB: they begin the task (S1), then Leo leads Salzman to the table (D), Leo sits and composes himself (A), Salzman takes out the cards (C), and then flips through them while Leo looks away (B), before the reflective close (S2).

Why other options are wrong: Alternative sequences place actions (cards/flipping) before the scene is set at the table/window or disrupt the cause-effect flow of actions.

Learning points: (1) Establish location before actions with objects. (2) Follow chronological action: lead → sit → take out → flip through. (3) Pronoun references (“he”) must have a clear antecedent. (4) Maintain smooth narrative progression. (5) End with the reflective/atmospheric sentence.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. At this moment I have failed in courtesy towards you, but I now beg of you, in the name of that God who has given you such great dexterity in arms, tell me who you are, and to what noble princes are you allied? questionsEn.s:
The best sequence is BDAC: after Khaled sees her (S1), they exchange salutes (B), then he begins speaking (D), explains his admiration (A) and supports it with praise (C), and finally urges an answer (S2).

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences place the question/praise before the greeting/salute or disrupt the natural flow of dialogue (opening → request → compliment → insistence).

Learning points: (1) Dialogue usually follows greeting/action first. (2) “said Khaled” introduces his speech early. (3) Praise often supports a request. (4) End aligns with “Answer me…” (S2). (5) Maintain conversational logic.

Shortly after, a suitor who was favoured by Lord Stair, and still more so by his lady, paid his addresses to Miss Dalrymple. C. Lady Stair, a woman accustomed to universal submission (or even her husband did not dare to contradict her), treated this objection as a trifle and insisted upon her daughter yielding her consent to marry the new suitor, David Dunbar, son and heir to David Dunbar of Baldoon, in Wigtownshire. The correct sequence is DBAC: after the engagement is mentioned (S1), the solemn pledge is described (D), then the favoured suitor appears (B), the girl refuses and confesses (A), and Lady Stair forces the new match (C), leading to the lover’s letter (S2).

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences misplace the background pledge (D) or put Lady Stair’s insistence (C) before the refusal/confession (A), breaking cause-effect flow.

Learning points: (1) Place background/details near the event they explain. (2) Track cause → reaction → consequence. (3) Identify “trigger” actions (proposal, refusal, insistence). (4) Keep pronoun/reference clarity (who objected/insisted). (5) S1/S2 provide the frame—fit the middle accordingly.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Why other options are wrong: Other orders place “accordingly” (B) too early or break the logical chain from reason (D) → decision (C) → intention (A) → action/result (B).

Learning points: (1) “Accordingly” signals a result/action after a decision. (2) Reasons usually precede decisions. (3) Look for connectors like “therefore” that demand prior context. (4) Keep timeline: home → decision → meeting → drinking. (5) S2 is the outcome; place drinking-related build-up right before it.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences introduce “the other” (B) too early or separate closely linked details about the host (A, C, D), reducing coherence.

Learning points: (1) Move from general to specific. (2) Keep descriptions of the same person together. (3) “One…the other…” structure usually follows in order. (4) Physical posture details often follow identification. (5) End with a closing action/observation that matches S2.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The best sequence is DACB: after S1 (books scattered), D logically adds where the largest collection was; A follows with “That was no problem nowadays…” referring to accessing books; C adds a contrast (“But it was just possible…”) about marginalia; B then mentions Roland’s specific search, leading naturally to S2 about pleasure in reading what Ash read.

Why other options are wrong: Other orders break reference links like “That” (A) and “But” (C) or place Roland’s search (B) before establishing the collections/access context.

Learning points: (1) Track pronoun/reference words: “That,” “But,” “And.” (2) Place general setting before specifics. (3) Contrast markers (“But”) usually follow a prior statement. (4) “And Roland…” fits after context is set. (5) Ensure S2 feels like a concluding reflection.

Learning points: (1) Establish setting/action first (entry via hole). (2) Then general description (“in every tree”). (3) Reactions/consequences follow (trees glad). (4) Wider scenic details often come later (birds/flowers). (5) End with a summary/contrast sentence (S2).

The sequence DACB maintains narrative order: first they sail and spot an island (D), then steer to it and land (A), then head toward a mountain (C), and finally reach the summit and find pits (B), leading into S2 about a mine of jewels.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences misplace “landed upon it” before the island appears, or place the mountain journey before reaching the island, breaking cause-effect flow.

Learning points: (1) Track travel stages: sail → island appears → land → move inland → reach summit. (2) Pronouns like “this/it” need clear antecedents. (3) Look for time markers (“sailed for three months”, “soon landed”, “after some hours”). (4) Ensure logical geography progression. (5) S2 should be supported by “pits/mine” just before it.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. He remained perplexed and confounded until the morning, when a eunuch advanced to him and said to him, May Allah grant a happy morning to the Prince of the Faithful! C. Yea, by Allah, answered the eunuch; thou art at this present time the Prince of the Faithful and the caliph of the Lord of all creatures. D.
