CADB fits best: after S1’s question, the eunuch confirms he is the Prince (C), then Abou Hassan reacts in amazement (A), then he expresses the yesterday/today contrast (D), and finally the morning scene of being greeted as Prince (B) aligns with his continued perplexity before S2’s gift episode.

Why other options are wrong: Sequences placing (B) too early disrupt the direct question–answer exchange in S1; others misplace the reaction lines (A/D) away from the confirmation (C).

Learning points: (1) Dialogue pairs: question → answer should stay together. (2) Reaction statements follow the confirmation. (3) Time cues (“until the morning”) usually come after initial night confusion. (4) Keep coherence of speaker and scene. (5) Ensure S2 follows a settled “Prince” setting.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Saidjah, who was then about seven, soon made friends with the new buffalo. A. Such a friendship the little Saidjah had soon been able to make with the newcomer; and it seemed as if the encouraging voice of the child gave more strength to the heavy shoulders of the animal, when it tore open the stiff clay and traced its way in deep sharp furrows. B. Of this attachment I shall soon give an example. C. The large strong animal bends its heavy head to the right, to the left, or downwards, just as the pressure of the child's finger directs. D. I purposely say “made friends,” for it was indeed touching to see how the buffalo was attached to the little boy who watched over and fed him. S2. The buffalo turned willingly on reaching the end of the field, not losing an inch of ground when plowing backwards the new furrow, which was ever near the old, as if the sawah was a garden ground raked by a giant.

DBCA is coherent: the narrator clarifies “made friends” (D), promises an example (B), then describes the buffalo’s obedience to the child’s guidance (C), and finally shows the friendship in action while ploughing (A), leading naturally to S2’s continued field description.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences place the “example” promise (B) after giving the example, or place detailed action (A/C) before the narrator’s clarification (D), weakening flow.

Learning points: (1) Authorial comment/clarification often comes early. (2) “I shall soon give an example” must precede the example. (3) General description can precede specific action. (4) Maintain cause → illustration order. (5) Connect S2 with ploughing context introduced just before it.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Flaw: Number Two is that deterrence is premised on fear. A. On the contrary, it is the endless, tireless, confrontational work of those who have had the courage to openly denounce them, the marches, the demonstrations, the films, the outrage-that is what has averted, or perhaps only postponed, nuclear war. B. It is not some inherent, mystical attribute of nuclear bombs that they automatically inspire thoughts of peace. C. But fear is premised on knowledge. D. On an understanding of the true extent and scale of the devastation that nuclear war will wreak. S2. Deterrence will not and cannot work given the levels of ignorance and illiteracy that hang over our two countries like dense, impenetrable veils.
questionsEn.s:
The sequence C→D explains what fear depends on (knowledge and understanding of devastation), then B denies a mystical “peace” effect of bombs, and A contrasts by crediting activism for averting war; this leads logically to S2 about ignorance defeating deterrence.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences break the dependency chain “fear → knowledge → understanding,” or place the contrast (“On the contrary”) without a proper preceding claim.

Learning points: (1) Track connector words: “But,” “On,” “On the contrary.” (2) Keep cause–explanation together (C with D). (3) “On the contrary” needs a prior statement to contrast (fits after B). (4) End should align with S2’s conclusion about ignorance. (5) Build the paragraph around the main idea introduced in S1.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Under pressure, it evolved and adapted. C. D sets the banyan as the focus and its ascendancy, B follows with adaptation under pressure, A gives a concrete growth behavior, and C expands this into the detailed process culminating in dominance—then S2 concludes with unmatched complexity.

Why other options are wrong: The wrong sequences either introduce detailed growth mechanics before establishing banyan’s dominance (D) or disrupt the general-to-specific flow.

Learning points: (1) Move from general context (S1) to main subject (D). (2) Cause/pressure → adaptation (B). (3) Short detail (A) can precede longer elaboration (C). (4) Keep the most descriptive/long sentence near the end before the conclusion. (5) Ensure S2 feels like a natural wrap-up.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. In the village of Sittendorf in Germany there dwelt, a long time ago, a poor but worthy man whose name was Peter Klaus. A. He could not have been persuaded for all the money in the world to spend his days in a shop tinkering at a trade. B. He liked to be out of doors. C. All the people for miles around knew Peter. D. He was not fond of hard work. S2. He liked to wander at his ease in the fields and the woods, enjoying the sunlight and the flowers and the songs of the birds.

C naturally follows the introduction by expanding on Peter’s familiarity; D states his dislike for hard work, A explains that he wouldn’t stay in a shop, and B leads directly into S2 about wandering outdoors.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences place “out of doors” too early or insert the shop-detail before stating his general attitude toward work, reducing coherence.

Learning points: (1) After introducing a person, a general remark often follows (C). (2) General trait (D) → supporting detail (A). (3) “Out of doors” (B) should connect smoothly to S2’s outdoor wandering. (4) Prefer general-to-specific order. (5) Look for sentences that act as bridges to S2.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. His face is ruddy, and he jokes about being a whiskey priest, though he's not. C. He has a decade on me; he's sixty-four, a big man, bald on top with grey at the sides; when he had hair, it was black. D. The sequence CBDA is coherent: C introduces who Father Paul is (age/appearance), B adds descriptive detail (ruddy face/jokes), D describes his current activities with the narrator, and A contrasts by noting he can’t be put on a horse anymore—leading smoothly into S2 about trail rides ten years ago.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences either place the contrast (A) too early or break the descriptive flow from identity → traits → activities → contrast before the past reference in S2.

Learning points: (1) Start with identification/background (often sentence with age/description). (2) Follow with additional traits/details. (3) Then actions/habits. (4) Place contrast words like “But” after some build-up. (5) Use S2 as a timeline anchor.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. B. When the old soldier returned and sat down again opposite to me at the table, we had the room to ourselves. C. Whatever their motive might be, at any rate they went away in a body. D. With one accord they all rose to depart. S2. I could see the croupier, in a sort of vestibule which opened out of it, eating his supper in solitude.

The sequence DACB works best: D shows the immediate reaction (they rose to depart), A gives the reason/assumption about their motive, C generalises the outcome (they went away together), and B states the resulting situation (room to ourselves), which leads naturally into S2 observing the croupier alone.

Why other options are wrong: Starting with B or C before the departure action (D) weakens cause–effect flow; A fits better after the departure is mentioned as an explanation of why they left.

Learning points: (1) Look for “action first” lines after a trigger in S1. (2) Explanations (“Probably…”) often follow the action. (3) Summary lines (“Whatever… at any rate…”) consolidate. (4) Consequence lines (“we had the room…”) set up S2. (5) Maintain time order.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. Why other options are wrong: Other sequences disrupt reference continuity (especially the introduction of “this sack”) and break the logical progression from setting to action to outcome.

Learning points: (1) Start with setting/context after S1 when given. (2) Maintain pronoun/reference links (e.g., “this sack”). (3) Prefer chronological action order. (4) Ensure each sentence naturally leads to the next. (5) Check cohesion through repeated nouns (cellar, sack, bodies).

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Although he was married, with children, his was a solitary disposition; he liked best to work alone. A. Autumn was best for this, better than spring. B. It pleased him when he was given a bank to build up or a gate to mend at the far end of the peninsula, where the sea surrounded the farmland on either side. C. Then, at midday, he would pause and eat the pasty that his wife had baked for him and, sitting on the cliff's edge, would watch the birds. D. In spring the birds flew inland, purposefully, intent; they knew where they were bound; the rhythm and ritual of their life brooked no delay. S2. In autumn those that had not migrated overseas but remained to pass the winter were caught up in the same driving urge, but because migration was denied them, followed a pattern of their own.
questionsEn.s:
“BCAD” is coherent: B explains the kind of work he liked; C continues with his midday routine; A introduces that autumn suited this; D contrasts with spring bird behavior, leading naturally to S2 about autumn birds’ different pattern.

Why other options are wrong: Other orders introduce “autumn/spring” comparisons without setup or break the seasonal contrast needed before S2.

Learning points: (1) Look for time markers: “Then,” “Autumn,” “In spring.” (2) Place “Then” after an activity is introduced. (3) Seasonal contrast must be built before a seasonal conclusion. (4) Ensure S2’s “In autumn…” is prepared by earlier autumn references. (5) Coherence depends on logical narrative flow.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. The staircase window having been boarded up, no light came down into the hall. A. Now the prosaic woman, looking about her, was more perplexed than she knew by everything that she saw, by traces of her long former habit of life-the yellow smoke stain up the white marble mantelpiece, the ring left by a vase on the top of the escritoire; the bruise in the wallpaper where, on the door being thrown open widely, the China handle had always hit the wall. B. Though not much dust had seeped in, each object wore a film of another kind; and, the only ventilation being the chimney, the whole drawing room smelled of the cold hearth. C. But one door, she could just see, stood ajar, so she went quickly through into the room and unshuttered the big window in there. D. The piano, having gone away to be stored, had left what looked like claw marks on its part of the parquet. S2. Mrs. Drover put down her parcels on the escritoire and left the room to proceed upstairs; the things she wanted were in a bedroom chest.
questionsEn.s:
“CADB” fits best: C moves the action into the room and opens the window; A and D detail what she notices inside; B adds atmosphere and condition of the room, leading to S2 where she uses the escritoire and leaves upstairs.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences either start with detailed observations before the entry/action (C) or place atmospheric description in a way that interrupts the observation flow.

Learning points: (1) Action/movement sentences often precede detailed descriptions. (2) Keep observation details grouped (A, D). (3) Place general atmosphere (B) after key visuals are introduced. questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence. **S1.** The grandmother didn't want to go to Florida. **A.** Bailey was the son she lived with, her only boy. **B.** "Now look here, Bailey," she said, "see here, read this," and she stood with one hand on her thin hip and the other rattling the newspaper at his bald head. **C.** He was sitting on the edge of his chair at the table, bent over the orange sports section of the Journal. **D.** She wanted to visit some of her connections in east Tennessee and she was seizing at every chance to change Bailey's mind. **S2.** "Here this fellow that calls himself The Misfit is aloose from the Federal Pen and headed toward Florida and you read here what it says he did to these people.
questionsEn.s:
The correct sequence is DACB. After S1 introduces the grandmother's reluctance to go to Florida, sentence D explains why—she wanted to visit Tennessee and tried to change Bailey's mind. A introduces Bailey as her only son. C describes Bailey sitting at the table reading the newspaper. B shows the grandmother trying to convince him by rattling the newspaper at him. This flows naturally into S2 where she mentions The Misfit.

Why other options are wrong: CBDA, BDAC, and ACBD do not maintain logical narrative flow. The grandmother's motivation (D) should come before identifying Bailey (A), followed by the scene description (C) and her action (B).

Learning points: (1) Start with motivation before action. (2) Introduce characters before describing their actions. (3) Physical descriptions precede dialogue. (4) Chronological order matters in narrative sequencing. (5) The final sentence should connect smoothly with S2.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence. **S1.** An old man came up to me in the fog. **A.** The people here call him insane. **B.** I know him well. **C.** He lives alone in a little house buried deep in the forest and has a small dog he carries always in his arms. **D.** "He is a little cracked," they say. **S2.** On many mornings I have met him walking on the road and he has told me of men and women who were his brothers and sisters, his cousins, aunts, uncles, brothers-in-law.
questionsEn.s:
The correct sequence is BADC. After S1 introduces the old man, sentence B states the narrator knows him well. A mentions that people call him insane. D provides the specific quote "He is a little cracked," which elaborates on sentence A. C gives descriptive details about how he lives. This flows naturally into S2, which describes the narrator's encounters with him.

Why other options are wrong: ADBC starts with what people say before establishing the narrator's acquaintance. DCBA and BCAD place the living description before establishing the context of insanity, disrupting logical flow.

Learning points: (1) Personal connection comes before public opinion. (2) General statement before specific quote. (3) Character traits before lifestyle details. (4) Build description from abstract to concrete. (5) Maintain coherent narrative progression.

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. Then, one day, she was up, playing; Isabel was in the kitchen fixing lunch for the two boys when they'd come in from school, and she heard Grace fall down in the living room. A. And she ran to the living room and there was little Grace on the floor, all twisted up, and the reason she hadn't screamed was that she couldn't get her breath. B. When you have a lot of children you don't always start running when one of them falls, unless they start screaming or something. C. Yet, Isabel says that when she heard that thump and then that silence, something happened in her to make her afraid. D. And, this time, Grace was quiet. S2. And when she did scream, it was the worst sound, Isabel says, that she'd ever heard in all her life, and she still hears it sometimes in her dreams.
questionsEn.s:
The logical flow is: general situation (B) → unusual silence (D) → fear due to thump and silence (C) → scene in living room explaining why no scream yet (A), before S2 mentions the eventual scream.

Why other options are wrong: Other sequences misplace the general statement (B) or the “this time” reference (D), breaking coherence and cause-effect progression.

Learning points: (1) Place general statements early to set context. (2) “This time” must follow a comparison/context. (3) Cause-effect: thump+silence → fear → discovery. (4) Pronoun/reference tracking improves ordering. (5) Ensure S2’s “when she did scream” is prepared by “couldn’t get her breath.”

questionsEn.q: Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.** S1. In old times there was a certain petty monarch by the name of Jayadatta, and there was born to him a son named Devadatta. A. Therefore, I will take a wife to my son from a merchant's family, in order that misfortune may not overtake his throne, though it is surrounded with many relations." B. "The prosperity of kings is very unstable, being like a courtesan to be enjoyed by force; but the prosperity of merchants is like a woman of good family; it is steady and does not fly to another man." C. And that wise king, wishing to marry his son, who was grown up, thus reflected: D. Having formed this resolve, that king sought for his son the daughter of a merchant in Pataliputra named Vasudatta. S2. Vasudatta for his part, eager for such a distinguished alliance, gave that daughter of his to the prince, though he dwelt in a remote foreign land.
questionsEn.s:
After introduction (S1), the king reflects (C), then gives the reasoning about merchants vs kings (B), then concludes the decision (A), and finally acts on it by seeking Vasudatta (D), leading to S2.

Learning points: (1) Reflection/setup lines often precede quoted reasoning. (2) A decision (“Therefore…”) follows reasons. (3) Actions (“Having formed this resolve…”) follow decisions. (4) Maintain logical chronology: think → decide → act. (5) Use connectors like “Therefore” and “Having formed this resolve” as ordering clues.

questionsEn.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions: Habits, scientists say, emerge because the brain is constantly looking for ways to save effort. Left to its own devices, the brain will try to make almost any routine into a habit, because habits allow our minds to ramp down more often. This effort-saving instinct is a huge advantage. An efficient brain requires less room, which makes for a smaller head, which makes childbirth easier, and therefore makes survival more likely. But conserving mental effort is only part of the story. Habits also have a powerful impact on our behaviors because once they are formed, they operate automatically. Even more importantly, habits can be changed, replaced, or ignored-but only if we understand how they work. At the core of every habit is a neurological loop that consists of three parts: a cue, a routine, and a reward. This loop is the foundation of all habitual behaviors. The cue is the trigger that tells your brain to go into automatic mode, the routine is the behavior itself, and the reward is what helps your brain remember the loop in the future. Understanding this loop is the first step in taking control of habits, whether you want to break a bad habit or create a new one. Rearrange the following sentences in correct order to make a meaningful passage.

1. The raw data was first compiled from field reports.
2. Charts and graphs were generated for visual clarity.
3. The data was then filtered for inconsistencies.
4. A final summary was submitted to the board.
questionsEn.s: Correct option (b) 1-3-2-4

questionsEn.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions: "The truth of the self-conscious individual lies not in its immediate certainty, but in the dialectical movement of its becoming. Consciousness, in its pursuit of knowledge, initially assumes that its object is something external and independent. Yet, through the labor of experience, it discovers that this object is not truly separate but is mediated by consciousness itself. The apparent duality of subject and object is thus sublated in the dialectic, revealing that knowledge is not the passive reception of an external truth but an active process in which consciousness shapes and transforms its own reality. This movement unfolds through a series of contradictions, in which each stage of consciousness, believing itself to have attained certainty, encounters its own inadequacy. The master-slave dialectic exemplifies this: self-consciousness seeks recognition from another, yet in asserting its dominance over the other, it paradoxically undermines its own freedom. The master, in reducing the slave to a mere instrument, deprives himself of a fully realized recognition. Meanwhile, the slave, through labor and self-transformation, attains a deeper awareness of autonomy, demonstrating that freedom is not given but achieved through negation and overcoming. questionsEn.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions: "The explanation of a work is always sought in the man or woman who produced it, as if it were always, in the end, through the voice of a single person that literature spoke: through the voice of a single person and the imprints of his or her passions. The image of literature that we seek to sustain is tyrannically centered on the author, his life, his history, and his intentions. But to give a text an Author is to impose a limit on that text, to furnish it with a final signified, to close the writing. Such a conception is born of the rationalist and capitalist ideologies that have placed the individual at the center of history, emphasizing his authority and coherence. Yet, in reality, writing is a destruction of every voice, of every point of origin. Writing begins at the moment the Author is set aside, and language speaks-not the Author. To refuse the Author is not to refuse meaning, but to refuse the tyranny of a single, authoritative meaning. The text, instead, becomes a space of multiple interpretations, where meaning is neither fixed nor final. The unity of a text is not located in its origin but in its destination; it is the reader, not the Author, who gives meaning to a text. This radical displacement shifts the power from the creator to the interpreter, from the supposed intention of the writer to the infinite play of signifiers within the text itself. Rearrange the following sentences in correct order to make a meaningful passage.

1. The candidate was asked to provide valid identification.
2. Her fingerprints were scanned and verified against the database.
3. She was escorted to the interview room after verification.
4. The security desk logged her entry into the visitor register.
questionsEn.s: Correct option (c) 1-4-2-3

questionsEn.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions: "Normal science, the activity in which most scientists inevitably spend almost all their time, is based on the assumption that the scientific community knows what the world is like. Scientists take great pains to defend that assumption, often restricting their vision to the phenomena that the existing paradigm has defined as relevant. When research proceeds in this fashion, findings tend to be incremental, reinforcing the established framework rather than challenging it. Yet, over time, anomalies-empirical observations that cannot be explained within the current paradigm-accumulate. Initially, these anomalies are dismissed as errors or as problems to be solved within the existing theoretical structure. However, as these anomalies grow in number and significance, they begin to erode confidence in the prevailing paradigm. The resolution of such crises is not a straightforward process of falsification, as Popper might suggest, but rather a transformation in the very way scientists see the world. Scientific revolutions occur when a new paradigm emerges-one that is not merely an extension of the old but a fundamental reconceptualization of reality. This shift is not purely logical or empirical; it involves a radical change in perspective, akin to a gestalt switch. The Copernican Revolution, for example, did not merely adjust astronomical calculations; it redefined the very framework through which celestial motion was understood. Similarly, Einstein's theory of relativity did not just modify Newtonian mechanics but replaced its foundational assumptions about space and time. Rearrange the following sentences in correct order to make a meaningful passage.

2. Original pages are uploaded in image format.

4. The output is saved in a searchable PDF format.

questionsEn.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions: The argument of this book is that we, and all other animals, are machines created by our genes. Like successful Chicago gangsters, our genes have survived sometimes for millions of years in a highly competitive world. This has entailed ruthless selfishness in gene selection, yet paradoxically it has also favored behaviors that, at an organismal level, may appear cooperative or even altruistic. The key to understanding this paradox lies in recognizing that what matters is not the survival of the individual organism, nor even the species, but rather the continuity of the genes themselves. Natural selection, therefore, operates at the level of replicators-genes-rather than the individual creatures they construct as temporary vehicles. These survival machines, whether they be humans, ants, or oak trees, serve merely as the means through which genes propagate. This gene-centered view of evolution helps explain many otherwise puzzling phenomena in nature. For example, kin selection provides a compelling reason why apparent acts of altruism, such as worker ants sacrificing their ability to reproduce, can evolve: by ensuring the survival and reproduction of closely related individuals, an organism still promotes the continuity of its genetic lineage. This perspective challenges the common anthropocentric tendency to view evolution as a process geared toward the 'good of the species. In reality, natural selection cares nothing for abstract collective welfare; it blindly favors gene variants that are better at replicating, regardless of their consequences beyond that singular goal. Rearrange the following sentences in correct order to make a meaningful passage.

1. The blueprint is finalized after approval from stakeholders.
2. First, a basic framework is proposed.
3. Then revisions are made after discussions.
4. Finally, execution begins as per plan.

Which of the given options is the most logical sequencing of the following sentences to form a meaningful paragraph?

1. He co-founded Apple Inc. along with Wozniak.
2. Steve Jobs was a visionary entrepreneur and innovator.
3. His ideas continue to influence modern technology and design.
4. Apple Inc. introduced products like iPhone and iPad.
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is Option 2.

Key Points

• The paragraph should begin with an introduction to Steve Jobs, providing an overarching description of who he was. Hence, sentence 2 comes first.

• The next logical step is to highlight his major achievement, which is co-founding Apple Inc. This makes sentence 1 the second sentence.

• Following that, we should discuss Apple's contributions, such as introducing products like the iPhone and iPad. Hence, sentence 4 comes next.

• Finally, the paragraph concludes by emphasizing the lasting influence of Steve Jobs' ideas, which is covered in sentence 3.

Therefore, the correct sequence is 2-1-4-3, and the correct answer is Option 2.

Correct Sequence: "Steve Jobs was a visionary entrepreneur and innovator. He co-founded Apple Inc. along with Wozniak. Apple Inc. introduced products like iPhone and iPad. His ideas continue to influence modern technology and design."

Additional Information

• Option 1: 3-1-2-4 – This sequence is incorrect because it begins with the influence of Steve Jobs' ideas (sentence 3), without introducing who he was.

• Option 3: 1-2-4-3 – This sequence is incorrect because it starts with co-founding Apple Inc. (sentence 1), which skips a proper introduction to Steve Jobs.

• Option 4: 4-3-1-2 – This sequence is illogical because it begins with Apple's products (sentence 4) without introducing Steve Jobs or his role first.

• Option 2: 2-1-4-3 – This sequence is correct as it logically introduces Steve Jobs, his achievements, Apple's contributions, and his lasting influence.

questionsEn.q:
Which of the given options is the most logical sequencing of the following sentences to form a meaningful paragraph?

1. His observations eventually contributed to his groundbreaking book, On the Origin of Species.
2. The Galápagos Islands are famous for their diverse wildlife and their role in Charles Darwin's theory of evolution.
3. This led him to propose the idea of natural selection, where species evolve over time to adapt to their environment.
4. Darwin observed that finches on different islands had distinct beak shapes suited to their specific diets.
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is Option 3.

Key Points

• The paragraph is about the Galápagos Islands and their significance in Charles Darwin's theory of evolution.

• Sentence 2 introduces the topic by mentioning the Galápagos Islands and their connection to Darwin's theory of evolution.

• Sentence 4 builds on this by describing Darwin's observation of finches with distinct beak shapes on different islands.

• Sentence 3 logically follows, explaining how Darwin's observations led to the concept of natural selection.

• Sentence 1 concludes the paragraph by mentioning how these observations contributed to his famous book, On the Origin of Species.

Therefore, the most logical sequence is 2-4-3-1, and the correct answer is Option 3.

Correct Paragraph: "The Galápagos Islands are famous for their diverse wildlife and their role in Charles Darwin's theory of evolution. Darwin observed that finches on different islands had distinct beak shapes suited to their specific diets. This led him to propose the idea of natural selection, where species evolve over time to adapt to their environment. His observations eventually contributed to his groundbreaking book, On the Origin of Species."

Additional Information

• Option 1 (2-4-1-3) is incorrect because sentence 1 prematurely concludes the paragraph before explaining Darwin's concept of natural selection.

• Option 2 (4-2-3-1) is incorrect as it disrupts the logical flow by starting with an observation instead of introducing the topic.

• Option 4 (1-3-2-4) is incorrect because it starts with the conclusion and ends abruptly without a proper introduction to the topic.

The collected data is then processed and analyzed centrally (Step Q), and the finalized report is shared publicly (Step S). This logical order ensures the census is executed systematically.

questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage : The proliferation of social media has fundamentally transformed the democratic landscape, acting both as a catalyst for civic engagement and a conduit for manipulation. Platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram, once relegated to the domain of personal expression, now serve as powerful instruments of political discourse, enabling citizens to articulate opinions, mobilize for causes, and scrutinize authority in real-time. At its core, democracy thrives on the free flow of information, and social media ostensibly democratizes this process by dismantling traditional gatekeeping. Political leaders communicate directly with constituents, bypassing editorial filters, while grassroots movements harness virality to amplify marginalized voices. During critical events—be it elections, protests, or legislative debates—social media acts as a digital agora, fostering participatory dialogue that was once confined to town halls or print columns. However, this unprecedented openness is double-edged. The same platforms that disseminate truth can also propagate misinformation, polarize public opinion, and algorithmically reinforce ideological silos. Electoral interference through fake accounts, coordinated trolling, and the spread of disinformation campaigns have threatened electoral integrity in several democracies. Moreover, emotionally charged content, optimized for engagement rather than accuracy, often eclipses nuanced debate, reducing political discourse to a cacophony of outrage. The role of social media in democracy, therefore, is contingent not just on its technological architecture, but on the ethical frameworks governing its use. Regulatory oversight, media literacy, and algorithmic transparency are essential to harness its democratic potential while mitigating its subversive tendencies. In essence, social media is neither inherently virtuous nor inherently corrosive—it is a mirror of societal intent. Whether it becomes a pillar of democratic resilience or a tool of populist distortion depends largely on how it is wielded by citizens, institutions, and platforms alike What primary democratic function does social media serve, as per the paragraph?
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is: Facilitating free flow of information.
Social media primarily serves a democratic function by enabling unrestricted sharing and access to information, fostering transparency and participation as per the paragraph.

questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage : Group thinking, often referred to as groupthink, is a psychological phenomenon wherein the desire for unanimity within a group overrides the motivation to appraise alternative viewpoints critically. It frequently leads to flawed decision-making because dissent is either internally suppressed or socially penalized. Social conformity, its close ally, describes the act of aligning one's beliefs or behaviours with those of a majority, often subconsciously, in pursuit of acceptance or avoidance of conflict. In tightly knit groups—such as corporate boards, political committees, or academic panels—individual members may refrain from expressing contrarian ideas, fearing ostracization or reputational risk. questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage: For seventeen-year-old Meera, adolescence was not merely a phase of hormonal transitions and academic aspirations—it became an arena where perception and self-worth collided with insidious intensity. In a world saturated with curated digital aesthetics and algorithm-driven beauty hierarchies, Meera’s own reflection began to feel less like truth and more like betrayal. Every scroll through her social media feed deepened a gnawing dissonance: between her authentic self and the impossible silhouettes idolized online. This wasn’t mere teenage insecurity—it manifested as a systematic devaluation of her physical self. Gradually, she adopted punitive behaviors: food became conditional, mirrors became adversaries, and compliments transformed into cryptic reminders of inadequacy. The subtle descent into dysmorphia was neither loud nor linear. Academically capable and socially pleasant, Meera wore the mask of normalcy with precision. Yet beneath the practiced smiles was a quiet implosion. She began withdrawing emotionally, rationalizing her distress as vanity, and trivializing her worth. The turning point came not with drama, but with silence—a refusal to eat for days, which led to medical intervention. Therapeutic engagement introduced her to the concept of self-image distortion, and the emotional scaffolding required to rebuild her fractured sense of identity. Through sustained counseling, Meera disentangled societal impositions from intrinsic value. She began to internalize that beauty is not a monolith dictated by culture but a spectrum shaped by diversity, health, and self-compassion. Meera’s narrative is not a singular anomaly but a mirror to a larger epidemic— where teenagers battle unspoken wars behind flawless digital façades. Combating this requires more than awareness; it calls for critical media literacy, empathetic environments, and systemic redefinition of beauty norms that extend beyond superficial metrics. What does the phrase "gnawing dissonance" in the passage most likely refer to?
o: Her hunger due to skipped meals
Conflict between her inner worth and online ideals
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is: Conflict between her inner worth and online ideals.
The phrase "gnawing dissonance" reflects the emotional tension caused by conflicting feelings about her self-worth and the unrealistic standards portrayed online.

questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage: In contemporary discourse, the debate between entrepreneurship and conventional employment has gained remarkable traction. While traditional employment offers predictability, structured growth, and a defined career trajectory, entrepreneurship appeals to those seeking autonomy, innovation, and the potential for exponential returns. However, both paths are fraught with distinct advantages and inherent uncertainties. Employment, particularly within established organizations, provides financial stability, social recognition, and institutional support. Employees are not burdened with existential risks such as capital loss or market unpredictability. Instead, they operate within frameworks of responsibility and hierarchy, where risk is absorbed at higher managerial levels. For many, this structure offers psychological comfort and a clear roadmap for progression. Conversely, entrepreneurship demands resilience, resourcefulness, and a high tolerance for ambiguity. Entrepreneurs must navigate volatile markets, regulatory complexities, and the absence of assured income—challenges often underestimated by aspirants. Yet, for those with a risk appetite and creative acumen, entrepreneurship promises a unique form of fulfillment. It allows individuals to disrupt existing paradigms, build ventures from the ground up, and possibly shape industries. Societal perceptions further complicate the dichotomy. In many cultures, steady employment is seen as the hallmark of success, while entrepreneurial endeavors are often perceived as reckless or unstable—until they succeed. This perception, however, is gradually shifting as global startup ecosystems mature and innovation becomes synonymous with progress. The real decision, therefore, lies not in which path is superior but in aligning one's temperament, values, and long-term goals with the demands of each route. Entrepreneurship may offer liberation, but it is not without sacrifice. Employment may provide security, but it can come at the cost of creative constraint. A reflective, context-aware approach—not blind aspiration—is essential for navigating this professional crossroads. According to the passage, which quality is most crucial for entrepreneurs?
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is Option 2.

Key Points

• The passage explicitly outlines the specific traits required to succeed in the entrepreneurial path, contrasting them with the structured nature of employment.

• It states that entrepreneurship demands resilience, resourcefulness, and a high tolerance for ambiguity to handle challenges like volatile markets and the absence of assured income.

• Resilience is the ability to recover quickly from difficulties, which aligns with the "volatile markets" and "inherent uncertainties" mentioned in the text.

• Qualities like obedience and conformity are typically associated with working within the "frameworks of responsibility and hierarchy" found in conventional employment, not entrepreneurship.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Correct Sentence from Text: "Conversely, entrepreneurship demands resilience, resourcefulness, and a high tolerance for ambiguity."

Additional Information

• Option 1: Obedience - This contradicts the "autonomy" and "liberation" that the passage associates with being an entrepreneur.

• Option 3: Delegation - While important in management, this specific term is not mentioned in the passage as a core requirement for entrepreneurs.

• Option 4: Conformity - The passage notes that entrepreneurs "disrupt existing paradigms," which is the opposite of conforming to them.

Entrepreneurs must navigate volatile markets, regulatory complexities, and the absence of assured income—challenges often underestimated by aspirants. Yet, for those with a risk appetite and creative acumen, entrepreneurship promises a unique form of fulfillment. It allows individuals to disrupt existing paradigms, build ventures from the ground up, and possibly shape industries. Societal perceptions further complicate the dichotomy. In many cultures, steady employment is seen as the hallmark of success, while entrepreneurial endeavors are often perceived as reckless or unstable—until they succeed. This perception, however, is gradually shifting as global startup ecosystems mature and innovation becomes synonymous with progress. The real decision, therefore, lies not in which path is superior but in aligning one's temperament, values, and long-term goals with the demands of each route. Entrepreneurship may offer liberation, but it is not without sacrifice. Employment may provide security, but it can come at the cost of creative constraint. A reflective, context-aware approach—not blind aspiration—is essential for navigating this professional crossroads. What does the word "dichotomy" in the passage most nearly mean?
o: A clear division between two contrasting things
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is Option 3.

Key Points

• In the context of the passage, "dichotomy" refers to the sharp contrast or division between entrepreneurship and conventional employment.

• The author uses the word to describe how society views these two paths as opposites--one as the "hallmark of success" (employment) and the other as "reckless or unstable" (entrepreneurship).

• A dichotomy exists when a concept is split into two distinct, often contradictory or mutually exclusive parts.

• Therefore, Option 3 ("A clear division between two contrasting things") is the most accurate definition based on how the text sets these two professional routes against each other.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

• Option 1: A shared understanding - This suggests consensus or agreement, which is the opposite of a dichotomy (division).

• Option 2: A mutual advantage - While both paths have benefits, the word "dichotomy" focuses on their differences, not their shared perks.

• Option 4: A repeated pattern - This would be a "cycle" or "trend," whereas a dichotomy refers to a structural split between two ideas.

questionsEn.q:
Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage: India's tryst with the Olympic Games began in 1900, when Norman Pritchard, a British-Indian athlete, clinched two silver medals in athletics. However, it wasn't until the

1928 Amsterdam Olympics that India emerged as a formidable force in hockey, winning its first team gold. What followed was a golden era, where the Indian men's hockey team dominated the Olympic arena with eight gold medals between 1928 and 1980—an unmatched legacy. Despite this early excellence, India's Olympic journey has been riddled with inconsistencies. Post-1980, a conspicuous medal drought gripped the nation, exposing systemic inefficiencies: lack of infrastructure, inadequate training, and minimal grassroots scouting. Athletes often relied more on personal resilience than institutional support to achieve global recognition. The 21st century, however, has ushered in a phase of cautious optimism. With the establishment of bodies like the Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) and increased corporate sponsorship, Indian athletes now enjoy improved access to international-level coaching, nutrition, and psychological training. The medal tallies, though modest, have seen an upward trend—symbolized by Neeraj Chopra's historic gold in javelin at Tokyo
2020. What's most heartening is the diversification of sports. No longer confined to hockey and wrestling, India is now making strides in disciplines like badminton, shooting, boxing, and athletics. Equally noteworthy is the rising representation and success of Indian women athletes, who have frequently been the torchbearers in recent Olympic outings. Yet, challenges remain. The transition from potential to podium demands long-term investment, scientific sports management, and societal encouragement that transcends cricket-centric fandom. While India's Olympic identity is still evolving, the collective ambition is clearer than ever: to transform from a participant nation into a sporting powerhouse. When did India first win an Olympic team gold medal?
questionsEn.s: The correct answer is: 1928 Amsterdam. India won its first Olympic team gold medal in hockey during the 1928 Amsterdam Olympics, as indicated in the passage provided.

questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage: Cricket, as a sport, has continually evolved in response to changing audience preferences and technological advancements. Among its many formats, Test cricket and One Day Internationals (ODIs) represent two contrasting philosophies—one rooted in endurance and strategy, the other in dynamism and entertainment. Test cricket, often regarded as the pinnacle of the sport, is a format that unfolds over five days, demanding exceptional levels of patience, technique, and mental resilience. It offers players the opportunity to exhibit classical skills and tactical acumen, where the fluctuating tempo mirrors the rhythm of real life—unpredictable, slow-burning, and layered. For purists, Test cricket is an art form, rewarding not merely flamboyance but consistency and grit. In contrast, ODIs compress the drama into a single day. With limited overs, this format prioritizes aggressive batting, innovative bowling variations, and strategic field placements. The adrenaline-infused pace of ODIs appeals to a broader demographic, especially in an era of dwindling attention spans and time constraints. For broadcasters and advertisers, the shorter format offers commercial viability, making it a lucrative spectacle. However, critics argue that the commercialization of ODIs has come at the expense of depth and nuance. In pursuit of viewership, substance often gives way to spectacle. Conversely, defenders of Test cricket lament its declining audience, attributing it to an increasingly entertainment-driven sports culture. Yet, occasional high-stakes encounters—like the Ashes or India-Australia series—still manage to ignite global interest. The ongoing debate between formats is not merely about preference, but about the challenge lies in preserving the sanctity of Test cricket without undermining the accessibility of ODIs—a delicate balance that cricketing authorities must negotiate in the years ahead. Which of the following best captures the essence of Test cricket, as described in the passage?
o: It is long and often boring
It includes domestic and emotional elements
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is Option 2.

Key Points

• The passage describes Test cricket as a format that unfolds over five days, requiring patience, technique, and mental resilience.

• It highlights how the format mirrors the rhythm of real life, characterized by a slow-burning, layered, and unpredictable progression.

• The text emphasizes that Test cricket rewards consistency, strategic depth, and tactical acumen, making it an art form for purists.

• Therefore, the essence of Test cricket in the passage is best captured by its representation of complexity, endurance, and unpredictability.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "It is long and often boring" - The passage acknowledges the length of Test cricket but does not describe it as boring; instead, it emphasizes depth and strategy.

• Option 3: "It includes domestic and emotional elements" - The passage does not mention domestic or emotional aspects as defining features of Test cricket.

• Option 4: "It is nostalgic and traditional" - Although Test cricket is respected by purists, the passage focuses more on its strategic complexity and unpredictability rather than nostalgia.

• ODIs in the passage are contrasted with Test cricket as faster, commercially viable, and entertainment-oriented formats.

questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage : To bifurcate life into immutable dichotomies of joy and sorrow is to misread its most intrinsic rhythm. Human existence unfolds not as a linear progression of happiness or despair, but as a dynamic interplay where each emotion deepens the resonance of the other. The ecstasy of triumph is never as poignant as when preceded by failure; likewise, the pang of loss finds contour only because we have once cherished the presence of what is now absent. Joy and sorrow, then, are not adversaries but co-authors of the same narrative. From antiquity to modernity, philosophical traditions have acknowledged this existential polarity. The Stoics embraced the inevitability of suffering as a precursor to tranquility, while Eastern philosophies like Buddhism anchor themselves in the impermanence of all experiences. In both frameworks, the pursuit of enduring happiness necessitates an acceptance of transience. Without sorrow, joy would be indistinct—a flat and shallow sensation lacking contrast or value. This interdependence is vividly manifest in the mundane. The delight of spring is intensified by the memory of a harsh winter; the serenity of solitude is meaningful only to one who has tasted the cacophony of crowds. Even our personal growth often emerges from crucibles of pain—grief chisels depth into our emotional landscape, refining our capacity for empathy, resilience, and gratitude. To demand unbroken happiness is to seek a monochromatic life—an existence devoid of emotional texture. The beauty of being lies not in circumventing sorrow, but in embracing it as a necessary foil to joy. These twin sentiments coalesce to form the chiaroscuro of consciousness, rendering our lives more vivid, more intricate, more human. Which of the following best completes the analogy: Joy is to presence as sorrow is to -- ?
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is Option 3.

Key Points

• The passage explores the interdependence of emotions, specifically how one provides the necessary context for the other.

• The author explicitly links these concepts by stating: "the pang of loss finds contour only because we have once cherished the presence of what is now absent."

• In this logic, "presence" (cherishing something) is the source of joy, while "absence" (the loss of that presence) is the source of sorrow.

• The analogy follows a cause-and-effect relationship defined in the text: Joy arises from having (presence), and sorrow arises from no longer having (absence).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Correct Sentence from Text: "...the pang of loss finds contour only because we have once cherished the presence of what is now absent."

Additional Information

• Option 1: Freedom - While sorrow can lead to growth, the passage does not define sorrow as freedom; instead, it uses "presence" and "absence" as direct structural counterparts.

• Option 2: Anticipation - The passage discusses the "memory" of experiences (like winter or failure), but doesn't link sorrow specifically to the act of looking forward.

• Option 4: Stagnation - The text actually argues the opposite; it suggests sorrow leads to growth and "refining our capacity," which is the antithesis of stagnation.

questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage : To bifurcate life into immutable dichotomies of joy and sorrow is to misread its most intrinsic rhythm. Human existence unfolds not as a linear progression of happiness or despair, but as a dynamic interplay where each emotion deepens the resonance of the other. The ecstasy of triumph is never as poignant as when preceded by failure; likewise, the pang of loss finds contour only because we have once cherished the presence of what is now absent. Joy and sorrow, then, are not adversaries but co-authors of the same narrative. From antiquity to modernity, philosophical traditions have acknowledged this existential polarity. The Stoics embraced the inevitability of suffering as a precursor to tranquility, while Eastern philosophies like Buddhism anchor themselves in the impermanence of all experiences. In both frameworks, the pursuit of enduring happiness necessitates an acceptance of transience. Without sorrow, joy would be indistinct—a flat and shallow sensation lacking contrast or value. This interdependence is vividly manifest in the mundane. The delight of spring is intensified by the memory of a harsh winter; the serenity of solitude is meaningful only to one who has tasted the cacophony of crowds. Even our personal growth often emerges from crucibles of pain—grief chisels depth into our emotional landscape, refining our capacity for empathy, resilience, and gratitude. To demand unbroken happiness is to seek a monochromatic life—an existence devoid of emotional texture. The beauty of being lies not in circumventing sorrow, but in embracing it as a necessary foil to joy. These twin sentiments coalesce to form the chiaroscuro of consciousness, rendering our lives more vivid, more intricate, more human. In the context of the passage, what does the word chiaroscuro most likely mean?
o: A blend of light and shadow
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is Option 2.

Key Points

• Chiaroscuro is an artistic term (originating from Italian: chiaro meaning light, and oscuro meaning dark) that refers to the use of strong contrasts between light and dark.

• In the passage, the author uses this as a metaphor for the human mind, where joy represents "light" and sorrow represents "shadow."

• The author argues that these "twin sentiments coalesce" (come together) to make consciousness more "vivid" and "intricate," much like how a painter uses light and shadow to create depth in a portrait.

• The surrounding text mentions a "monochromatic life" (single color) as the opposite, reinforcing that the author is discussing a blend of contrasting elements.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Contextual Sentence from Text: "These twin sentiments coalesce to form the chiaroscuro of consciousness, rendering our lives more vivid, more intricate, more human."

Additional Information

• Option 1: Emotional paralysis - Incorrect. The author describes this state as "dynamic" and "vivid," which is the opposite of being paralyzed or stuck.

• Option 3: A musical variation - Incorrect. While "rhythm" and "resonance" are used earlier, "chiaroscuro" specifically belongs to the visual arts domain.

• Option 4: A specific type of sorrow - Incorrect. The term refers to the combination of joy and sorrow together, not just one side of the coin.

questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage : Art, in its manifold forms— visual, performative, literary, and auditory—constitutes a domain that transcends utilitarian function and enters the realm of the symbolic, the affective, and the transformative. Its significance within society cannot be reduced to decoration or diversion; rather, it operates as a mode of critical reflection, a vessel of collective memory, and a catalyst for socio-cultural evolution. At its core, art interrogates the contours of reality by reframing perception. Whether through the destabilizing surrealism of a Dali canvas or the dissonant harmonies of avant-garde music, art dislodges the observer from complacency and compels re-engagement with the world. It is in this function that art becomes not only an aesthetic but an epistemological act— challenging dominant paradigms and opening discursive space for marginalized narratives. Historically, art has served as an archive of civilizations, encoding within its mediums the aspirations, anxieties, and ideologies of its epoch. From the sacred iconography of temple frescoes to the protest murals adorning urban decay, art becomes a text through which power, resistance, and identity are simultaneously contested and constituted. This historical embeddedness renders art indispensable to understanding not only what a society creates but what it values and fears. In modern democracies, the role of art assumes a distinctly political dimension. Art enables dissent when speech is suppressed, and engenders empathy where rational argument fails. Satire, documentary film, and performance art often articulate the unspeakable, using metaphor and allusion to subvert censure. Yet this potential also renders art vulnerable—to censorship, commodification, and ideological co-option. When stripped of autonomy, art may devolve into propaganda or elitist ornamentation—devoid of critical function. The sociological function of art extends to its capacity to cultivate communal belonging and individual introspection simultaneously. Participatory forms of art—street theatre, public installations, folk traditions—dissolve the binaries of creator and audience, democratizing aesthetic engagement. Meanwhile, solitary encounters with a painting or a poem can occasion personal revelation, catharsis, or ethical inquiry. However, in the algorithmic age, where virality and visibility often dictate cultural value, art faces unprecedented commodification. The aesthetic is frequently reduced to a spectacle optimized for consumption, divorced from nuance, complexity, or transgression. The challenge, therefore, is to preserve the sanctity of artistic integrity in the face of market and media pressures that threaten to flatten it into banality. Ultimately, the role of art in society is neither static nor monolithic. It is a dialectical force—at once reflective and projective, disruptive and redemptive. To safeguard art is to safeguard the capacity of humanity to feel, to question, and to reimagine. What is implied by describing art as an "epistemological act" in the passage?
o: Art is a method of acquiring and challenging knowledge structures.
Art serves as mere historical documentation.
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is Option 2.

Key Points

• The passage defines art as an "epistemological act" because it "interrogates the contours of reality" and "challenges dominant paradigms."

• Epistemology is the study of knowledge; the text suggests art isn't just about beauty (aesthetics) but about how we perceive and know the world.

• By "dislodging the observer from complacency," art forces a "re-engagement with the world," which facilitates acquiring new perspectives and questioning established "knowledge structures."

• Option 2 accurately captures this intellectual and structural challenge, whereas the other options limit art to emotion, simple documentation, or propaganda.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Correct Sentence from Text: "It is in this function that art becomes not only an aesthetic but an epistemological act-- challenging dominant paradigms and opening discursive space for marginalized narratives."

Additional Information

• Option 1: Incorrect. While the text mentions art has an "affective" (emotional) realm, the "epistemological" label specifically refers to its role in knowledge and perception.

• Option 3: Incorrect. The passage states that art's significance "cannot be reduced to decoration" and goes beyond being a "vessel of collective memory" by being a catalyst for evolution.

• Option 4: Incorrect. The author warns that when art reflects state ideologies (propaganda), it is actually stripped of its autonomy and critical function.

questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has evolved from being a peripheral philanthropic gesture to an integral strategic imperative in contemporary business ecosystems. Modern corporations are increasingly cognizant of their multifaceted responsibilities—not only to shareholders but also to employees, consumers, communities, and the environment. This paradigm shift reflects a recognition that long-term profitability and sustainability are inextricably linked to ethical conduct and inclusive growth. CSR transcends token charity; it encompasses deliberate initiatives aimed at environmental stewardship, equitable labour practices, transparent governance, and community development. For instance, corporations may engage in afforestation drives, fund educational scholarships, ensure fair wages, or invest in renewable energy solutions. Such undertakings are not merely altruistic—they bolster corporate reputation, foster consumer loyalty, and mitigate regulatory risks. In some jurisdictions, like India, CSR has been legislated, mandating certain profit thresholds to be reinvested into socially beneficial projects, thereby institutionalizing moral capitalism. However, genuine CSR is distinguished from superficial public relations exercises by its intent, consistency, and impact measurement. Tokenistic CSR—where companies engage in isolated acts of giving to polish their public image—can often be counterproductive, exposing ethical hollowness when scrutinized. Conversely, purpose-driven CSR, embedded into core business strategies, can catalyze innovation and expand market reach, especially in underserved regions. Furthermore, stakeholders—particularly the socially conscious millennial and Gen Z demographics—now scrutinize corporate behaviour with unprecedented vigilance. With social media amplifying accountability, any dissonance between a company's stated values and its actions can provoke swift reputational damage. Therefore, CSR today is as much about risk mitigation as it is about value creation. Ultimately, the most impactful CSR initiatives are those that align profit motives with societal advancement. When businesses act not merely as economic entities but as responsible social agents, they contribute meaningfully to holistic progress, bridging the chasm between commerce and conscience. What does the author primarily convey about CSR in modern times?
o: It is mandated in all countries
It is central to business strategy
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is: It is central to business strategy.
The author highlights that CSR is now integrated into core business strategies, emphasizing its significance in driving sustainable growth and aligning with modern societal expectations.

questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage : Democracy is frequently extolled as the political system that best guarantees individual liberty. Enshrined in constitutional rights and protected by the rule of law, freedom of speech, association, religion, and conscience are regarded as hallmarks of democratic governance. However, what is less frequently acknowledged—but equally vital—is the reciprocal pillar of responsibility without which such freedoms can degenerate into chaos, polarization, or authoritarian backlashes. Freedom in a democracy is not absolute; it exists within a framework of mutual restraint and civic discipline. The right to express dissent, for instance, is foundational. Yet when freedom of expression is weaponized to disseminate hate speech, misinformation, or seditious propaganda, it ceases to serve the democratic cause. Responsibility thus entails a conscious engagement with the implications of one's actions—not just their legality, but their ethical and civic consequences. The challenge lies in reconciling liberty with accountability in pluralistic societies. With diverse cultural, ideological, and economic constituencies, democracies are inherently sites of contention. In such contexts, responsibility demands more than legal compliance—it requires empathy, critical thinking, and a commitment to collective well-being. A citizen's right to protest, for example, must be exercised with awareness of public order and respect for differing viewpoints. Similarly, the freedom to vote must be matched by an obligation to make informed choices, unswayed by populism, prejudice, or manipulation. The tension between freedom and responsibility is perhaps most visible during moments of crisis—be it a pandemic, a communal riot, or a constitutional standoff. In such times, the temptation to prioritize personal liberty at the cost of collective safety can prove fatal. Refusal to wear masks during a health emergency or the viral spread of unverified news during civil unrest exemplify how unbridled freedom can undermine democratic resilience. Moreover, democracy itself is not self-sustaining; it requires vigilant citizens who recognize that rights are not entitlements in perpetuity, but privileges preserved through active participation. When freedom is divorced from responsibility, democratic institutions become vulnerable to erosion—from within. Demagogues often rise not solely because of state failure, but due to civic apathy or irresponsible use of democratic freedoms by the populace itself. Therefore, in any functioning democracy, freedom and responsibility are not opposing forces but mutually reinforcing imperatives. The preservation of liberty necessitates a citizenry capable of ethical judgment, informed debate, and constructive dissent. In the absence of responsibility, freedom risks transforming from a catalyst of justice into a vehicle of division. Democracy survives not just through the laws it enacts, but through the civic virtues its citizens embody. According to the passage, what happens when freedom is exercised without responsibility?
o: It leads to misuse and societal harm
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is Option 3.

Key Points

• The passage emphasizes that without the "reciprocal pillar of responsibility," freedoms can "degenerate into chaos, polarization, or authoritarian backlashes."

• It specifically mentions that unbridled freedom can "undermine democratic resilience" and lead to the "viral spread of unverified news" or the "weaponization" of expression for hate speech.

• The author argues that when freedom is divorced from responsibility, institutions become vulnerable to erosion and can become a "vehicle of division."

• This clearly points to Option 3, as the result is misuse of rights and harm to the social fabric.

Therefore, the correct answer is 3.

Relevant Quote: "In the absence of responsibility, freedom risks transforming from a catalyst of justice into a vehicle of division."

Additional Information

• Option 1: The passage suggests that responsibility requires more than just legal compliance; it doesn't say irresponsible freedom enhances the system.

• Option 2: Irresponsible freedom is described as leading to "polarization" and "division," which is the opposite of strengthening unity.

• Option 4: The passage notes that demagogues rise and institutions erode when freedom is used irresponsibly, which actively harms governance.

questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage : In the relentless pursuit of excellence, the dichotomy between hard work and smart work emerges not merely as a matter of preference but as a nuanced dialectic in the broader schema of human productivity. Hard work—often equated with sheer diligence, indefatigable endurance, and linear perseverance—has historically been valorized as the cornerstone of achievement. The laboring individual, armed with nothing but obstinacy and time, is celebrated in folklore and biographies alike. However, in an era punctuated by algorithmic precision and cognitive economy, such traditional notions increasingly invite scrutiny. questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage : India's legacy of healing practices—embodied in disciplines such as Yoga, Ayurveda, Siddha, and Unani—presents a complex synthesis of philosophy, biology, and metaphysics. Far from being static relics of the past, these systems have exhibited an evolving dynamism, continuously negotiating their space within both indigenous frameworks and global health discourses. At the heart of this healing ethos lies the idea that the human body is not an isolated physiological entity but a site of interconnected energies and rhythms. Yoga, as codified in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, is not merely a physical regimen but a holistic path aimed at harmonizing the body, mind, and spirit. In the modern era, however, it has undergone commodification, particularly in the West, where its philosophical moorings are often diluted into mere physical exercise or stress-reduction techniques. This recontextualization, while facilitating global popularity, raises questions about cultural appropriation and epistemic erosion. Traditional medicine systems such as Ayurveda view disease as an imbalance in the tridosha—vata, pitta, and kapha—principles that regulate bodily function. These systems emphasize prakriti (constitution), ahara (diet), and dinacharya (daily routine) as central to preventive healthcare. Unlike allopathy's symptom-targeting approach, traditional Indian medicine is premised on restoring equilibrium in the body's internal ecology. This integrative vision aligns with contemporary calls for personalized and preventive medicine, though methodological differences continue to stoke skepticism in the biomedical community. State patronage of AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, and Homeopathy) underlines a renewed institutional interest in traditional systems. However, critics caution against uncritical endorsement, citing the lack of standardized clinical trials, variability in diagnostic models, and challenges in evidence-based validation. Furthermore, pharmaceutical commercialization of Ayurvedic formulations often sidelines traditional knowledge holders, reducing centuries-old practices to marketable commodities. The interface between Yoga and traditional medicine with modern healthcare is therefore both promising and fraught. While integrative models are being explored—especially in palliative care, mental health, and chronic disease management—they require epistemic humility and regulatory rigor. The danger lies in either romanticizing these systems as panaceas or discarding them as pre-scientific relics. Ultimately, the relevance of Yoga and traditional medicine in contemporary India will depend on the country's ability to safeguard their philosophical depth while subjecting them to transparent, rigorous scrutiny. Neither dogmatic revivalism nor dismissive scientism will suffice. What is needed is a dialogical framework where tradition and modernity coevolve—not in opposition, but in mutual enrichment What tension does the passage highlight regarding the global adoption of Yoga?
questionsEn.s:
The correct answer is Option 2: Loss of its philosophical essence.

Key Points

• The passage emphasizes that the global adoption of Yoga has led to a loss of its philosophical essence in some contexts.

• Yoga, traditionally rooted in spiritual and philosophical teachings, is often reduced to mere physical exercise in its globalized form.

• The commercialization and adaptation of Yoga for modern practices have diluted its original principles and deeper meanings.

• This shift highlights the tension between preserving Yoga's cultural heritage and adapting it to contemporary lifestyles.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Correct Explanation:  "Yoga, traditionally a holistic discipline integrating physical, mental, and spiritual practices, has often seen its philosophical roots overshadowed by its emphasis on physical postures in its global adaptation."

Additional Information

• Option 1: Lack of flexibility - While flexibility is associated with Yoga, the primary concern highlighted in the passage is not physical flexibility but the loss of its philosophical essence.

• Option 3: Shortage of teachers - The passage does not discuss the availability or shortage of Yoga instructors.

• Option 4: Over-regulation by India - There is no mention of regulation or over-regulation by India in the passage.

• Options involving antibiotics, synthetic drugs, or genetic mutation targeting reflect methods of modern medicine, not Ayurveda.

questionsEn.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on the passage: While financial inclusion is often praised as a driver of equitable growth, its implementation in rural India presents a paradox. On paper, schemes such as the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), Aadhaar-enabled payment systems, and mobile banking have revolutionized access. Yet, in practice, access does not necessarily translate into utility. A significant number of rural account holders remain dormant users, often constrained by digital illiteracy, infrastructural limitations, and deeply entrenched socio-cultural barriers. In numerous villages, banking correspondents (BCs)—the foot soldiers of India's rural financial architecture—are overburdened, undertrained, and often unsupported by robust technological infrastructure.
